tool.name: SQL
tool.tagline: The standard language for querying and managing relational databases
tool.description: SQL is the declarative language used to define, query and change data in relational databases such as PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle and SQLite. It is how backends, analysts and data tools talk to stored data, and it has outlived every trend for fifty years. This curriculum uses PostgreSQL as the reference dialect and notes where others differ.

glossary.def: A free, widely used database system that speaks SQL and follows the official standard closely. These lessons use its version of SQL.
A popular free database system that speaks SQL, common behind websites. Its SQL differs from PostgreSQL's in some details.
A small database system that keeps a whole database in one file and runs inside the app that uses it, with nothing separate to install. It is built into phones and browsers.
Microsoft's database system. It speaks its own version of SQL, called T-SQL.
Oracle Database: a commercial database system common in large companies, with its own version of SQL.
PostgreSQL's own text-based app: you type SQL after its prompt, and it prints the results as a simple table.
One database product's version of SQL. The core is the same everywhere, but details such as some function names and extra features differ.
The part of the database that decides how to carry out a query: which table to read first, whether to use an index, and so on. You say what you want; it works out the steps.
SQL's rule that a condition can be true, false or unknown (when NULL is involved). WHERE keeps only the rows where it is true.
One part of an SQL statement that starts with a keyword, such as the WHERE clause or the ORDER BY clause.
The part of a SELECT between SELECT and FROM: the columns and calculations each result row will contain.
The name of something in the database, such as a table or a column. In SQL, double quotes mark an identifier, as in "Order Total".
A temporary name you give a column or table inside a query with AS, e.g. price * 1.2 AS price_with_vat.
A rule attached to a table that the database checks on every change, such as NOT NULL (a value is required) or UNIQUE (no repeats). Changes that break it are rejected.
To make a transaction's changes permanent and visible to everyone, with the SQL statement COMMIT. Until then they can still be undone.
In SQL, a text template used with LIKE: % stands for any run of characters and _ for exactly one, so 'M%' means 'starts with M'.
The SQL statements that create or change the structure of a database (CREATE, ALTER, DROP), as opposed to those that read or change the data inside it.
A planned change to the structure of a database that is already in use, such as adding a column, usually saved as a file of SQL so it runs the same way everywhere.
A claim the database places on a row or table while a change is in progress, so others can't make a conflicting change at the same time. Anyone who needs it waits until it is released.
Paging through results by remembering the last row shown and asking for the rows after it, instead of skipping a count of rows with OFFSET. It stays fast however deep you go.
A key made of real-world data, such as a book's ISBN or a country code. Such values can change or be reused, which causes trouble.
A key with no real-world meaning, such as an id number the database generates. Because it means nothing, it never needs to change.
A column the database fills in automatically with the next number (1, 2, 3...) for each new row, usually used as the table's id.
A key made of two or more columns together, such as (order_id, product_id): no two rows may share the same combination.
The guarantee that every link between tables is valid: for example, every order's customer_id matches a customer that really exists.
How many rows on each side can be linked. One customer has many orders (one-to-many); a product has many tags and a tag many products (many-to-many).
Joining a table to itself under two different aliases, for example to pair up customers who live in the same city.
A query that finds rows with no match in another table, such as customers with no orders. Written with NOT EXISTS, or a LEFT JOIN plus IS NULL.
A query that keeps the rows that have at least one match in another table, each only once however many matches it has. Written with EXISTS or IN.
A SELECT written in parentheses inside another statement. The outer statement uses its result as a single value, a list or a table.
A subquery that returns exactly one value (one row, one column), so it can be used anywhere a single value can.
A subquery that refers to the current row of the outer query, so in principle it runs again for each outer row.
A subquery written in FROM and used like a temporary table by the rest of the query.
Turning values spread over rows into separate columns, e.g. one row per customer with one column per order status.
Reading every row of a table from start to end to find the matches. It is what happens when no index helps.
The default kind of index: values kept sorted in a shallow tree shape, so the database finds any value, or a range of values, in a handful of steps.
An index on several columns, sorted by the first column, then by the second within each value of the first, and so on.
An index on a calculated value, such as lower(email). Queries that filter on exactly that calculation can use it.
An index that contains only the rows matching a condition, such as only pending orders, so it stays small.
An index that also stores extra columns (added with INCLUDE), so some queries can be answered from the index without reading the table.
Answering a query entirely from an index, without reading the table itself.
A PostgreSQL index type for values that contain many items, such as JSON documents, lists and searchable text.
A PostgreSQL index type for ranges, shapes and locations, and for 'what is nearest?' searches.
A tiny PostgreSQL index that stores only the smallest and largest value for each block of the table. Useful for huge tables whose rows arrive in order, such as by time.
The default mode in which each statement is its own transaction and is saved as soon as it succeeds.
A named point inside a transaction that you can roll back to, undoing only the work done after it.
A common table expression: a named step written with WITH at the start of a query, which the rest of the query can use like a table.
A CTE that refers to itself, repeating a step on its own output until no new rows appear. Used to walk trees such as category hierarchies.
A function that calculates over a set of related rows, such as a running total or a rank, but keeps every row instead of collapsing them as GROUP BY does.
The rows of a window function's group that a calculation looks at for the current row, e.g. 'from the first row up to this one' for a running total.
Combining the results of two whole queries: stacking them (UNION), keeping rows found in both (INTERSECT) or removing one from the other (EXCEPT).
Designing tables so each fact is stored in exactly one place. Normal forms (1NF, 2NF, 3NF) are checklists for it; denormalization means copying data on purpose for speed.
A table that links two others in a many-to-many relationship, with one row per linked pair, such as (product_id, tag_id).
A piece of code the database runs automatically whenever rows in a particular table are inserted, updated or deleted.
PostgreSQL's column type for JSON, stored in a ready-to-search form that is fast to query and can be indexed.
Multi-version concurrency control: instead of changing a row in place, the database writes a new version of it, so readers keep seeing the old version until the change is committed.
One stored copy of a row. In PostgreSQL every UPDATE writes a new row version and marks the old one as expired; PostgreSQL's own word for it is tuple.
An old row version that no running transaction can see any more. It wastes space until VACUUM removes it.
PostgreSQL's cleanup job: it removes old row versions nobody can see any more so their space can be reused. Autovacuum runs it automatically in the background.

PostgreSQL numbers transactions with a counter that eventually runs out and starts again. VACUUM must mark old rows as safely old before then, or the database stops accepting changes to protect the data.
Wasted space in a table or index taken up by old row versions that haven't been cleaned up, making it bigger and slower to read.

A setting that controls how much transactions running at the same time see of each other's changes: Read Committed, Repeatable Read or Serializable. Stricter levels prevent more mistakes but make some transactions fail and need a retry.
Reading another transaction's changes before it has committed them, so you may act on data that is later undone. PostgreSQL never allows it.
Running the same query twice in one transaction and getting new rows the second time, because another transaction inserted them in between.
Two transactions read the same value, both change it and both save, so the first change is silently overwritten, e.g. two sales each setting stock from 5 to 4.
Two transactions each check a rule, both see it satisfied, then each changes different rows, and together they break the rule, e.g. two doctors both going off call.
A result that could not have happened if the transactions had run one after another; the strictest isolation level detects these and cancels one transaction.
A lock on a number you choose rather than on a row, used to coordinate your own programs, e.g. so only one copy of a nightly job runs at a time.
The share of rows a condition keeps. A condition matching 1% of rows is very selective, which is when an index pays off.
Extra statistics you ask PostgreSQL to collect about how columns relate (for example, city decides country), so its row estimates stay right for combined conditions.
A join method: for each row on one side, look up its matches on the other side, ideally with an index. Best when one side is small.
A join method: load the smaller table into a quick lookup structure in memory, then check each row of the bigger one against it. Good for large joins on equal values.
A join method: walk through both inputs sorted on the join column at the same time, pairing up matches, like merging two sorted lists.
A query plan PostgreSQL reuses for every run of a prepared statement, whatever values are passed, instead of planning each run for its actual values.
Skipping the partitions of a table that can't contain matching rows, because the query's filter on the partition key rules them out.
A moment when PostgreSQL writes all changed data from memory into its data files, so crash recovery only has to replay the log from that point on.
Restoring a database to any chosen moment, by starting from a full backup and replaying the saved log of changes up to that moment.
A full copy of a PostgreSQL server's data files: the starting point for point-in-time recovery or for a new replica.
Keeping a copy of a database on another server that continuously receives the original's write-ahead log and replays it, staying an exact copy.
Sending the row changes of chosen tables to another database, which applies them as ordinary inserts, updates and deletes.
A server that keeps a replicated copy of the main (primary) database, ready to take over if it fails. A hot standby also answers read-only queries.
A record on the primary server of how far a replica or other consumer has read, which makes the primary keep its log until that consumer has it.
A performance mistake where code runs one query to get a list, then one more query for every item in it, instead of a single query or join.

concepts.name: Databases and SQL
concepts.summary: A database stores data safely for many users at once; SQL is the language you use to ask it questions and change what it holds.
concepts.why: Almost every app, website and report gets its data from a database, and SQL is how people and programs talk to one.
concepts.body:
Picture a shop that keeps its customers, products and orders in a spreadsheet. That works until there are a million orders, several staff edit the file at once, and someone needs 'every order from London last March' within a second. A **database** is software built for exactly that: it stores large amounts of data, lets many people read and change it at the same time, and doesn't lose anything if the power fails.

**SQL** (say 'ess-cue-ell' or 'sequel') is the language you use to talk to a database. You write a short instruction in something close to English, and the database carries it out. For example, `SELECT name FROM customers;` asks for the name of every customer.

Each complete instruction is called a **statement**, and it ends with a semicolon `;`. A statement that asks a question and gets data back is a **query**. Other statements add, change or delete data, or create new places to store it.

In the examples, lines starting with two dashes `--` are comments: notes for the human reader that the database ignores. We use them to show what each query returns.

A database usually runs as a **server**: a program, often on another computer, that waits for instructions and answers them. You talk to it through a **client**, an app where you type SQL and see the results. PostgreSQL comes with a simple text client called **psql**; apps such as pgAdmin and DBeaver do the same job with windows and buttons.

Many database products understand SQL. The best known are **PostgreSQL**, **MySQL**, **SQLite**, Microsoft's **SQL Server** and **Oracle**. The core of the language is an international standard and works the same everywhere, but each product adds extras and differs in small details. So each speaks its own **dialect** of SQL.

These lessons use PostgreSQL, which is free and follows the standard closely, and point out where the others differ.
concepts.code:
-- A query: ask the database for data
SELECT name, city FROM customers;
--  name  | city
--  Ana   | Yerevan
--  Ben   | London
--  ...

-- Other statements change data; each ends with a semicolon
UPDATE customers SET city = 'Paris' WHERE name = 'Ana';

-- In psql you type a statement after the prompt and press Enter:
--   shop=> SELECT 2 + 3;
--    ?column?
--           5
takeaways: A database stores shared data safely and answers questions about it quickly
SQL is the language for talking to it: one instruction is a statement, a question is a query
Many products speak SQL in slightly different dialects; these lessons use PostgreSQL
pitfalls: Expecting SQL copied from a MySQL or SQL Server tutorial to run unchanged in PostgreSQL: the core works, but some details differ.

quiz.q: What is a query?
options: A statement that asks the database for data and gets rows back
The program that runs the database
quiz.explain: Any complete instruction is a statement; a query is the kind that asks for data and returns a result.

quiz.q: Why might SQL written for SQL Server need small changes before it runs in PostgreSQL?
options: SQL Server uses a completely different language
Each product speaks its own dialect: the core is shared, but some details differ
quiz.explain: SQL is a standard, but every product adds its own extras and spells some things differently.

concepts.name: Tables, rows and the relational model
concepts.summary: A relational database keeps data in tables of rows and columns, and links tables by storing matching id values.
concepts.why: Every SQL statement you will write reads or changes tables, so the picture of how tables fit together comes first.
concepts.body:
A **relational database** stores data in **tables** that look a lot like spreadsheet sheets. Each table holds one kind of thing: customers, products, orders. Each **row** is one of those things, such as one customer. Each **column** is one fact recorded for every row, such as the customer's name or email.

Throughout these lessons we use one small online shop with four tables. Each line below names a table, followed by its columns in brackets:

```sql
customers(id, name, email, city)
products(id, name, category, price)
orders(id, customer_id, status, total, ordered_at)
order_items(order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price)
```

Every column has a **data type**: the kind of value it may hold, such as whole numbers, decimal numbers, text or dates. `price` holds numbers and `name` holds text. The database refuses a value that doesn't fit, so nobody can put 'cheap' into `price` by accident.

Each row needs something that tells it apart from every other row. That is the job of the **primary key**: a column whose value is different for every row and never missing. In our shop it is the `id` column. Two customers may both be called Ana, but they will have different ids.

Tables are linked by storing those ids. An order doesn't contain a copy of the customer's details: its `customer_id` column holds the `id` of the customer who placed it. We write that column as `orders.customer_id`, meaning 'the customer_id column of the orders table'. When you need both, you ask SQL to match them up. Because links are just matching values, you can combine tables in ways nobody planned when they were designed.

The overall design (which tables exist, and which columns and types each has) is called the **schema**.

Sometimes a value simply isn't known. SQL marks that with `NULL`, meaning 'unknown' or 'missing'. In our data, Dev's city is NULL. It is not zero and not empty text, and a later lesson shows why that matters.

SQL is **declarative**: you describe the result you want, such as 'customers in London, sorted by name', not the steps to find it. A part of the database called the **query planner** works out the fastest way to get it. One more fact: rows have no built-in order. If you want them sorted, you must ask.
concepts.code:
-- The customers table: 4 rows, 4 columns
-- (SELECT, which reads data, is the next lesson)
SELECT * FROM customers;
--  id | name  | email             | city
--   1 | Ana   | ana@example.com   | Yerevan
--   2 | Ben   | ben@example.com   | London
--   3 | Chloe | chloe@example.com | London
--   4 | Dev   | dev@example.com   | NULL      <- unknown

-- orders.customer_id holds the id of the customer who ordered
SELECT id, customer_id, status, total, ordered_at FROM orders;
--  id  | customer_id | status    | total  | ordered_at
--  101 |           1 | shipped   |  68.50 | 2026-01-05
--  102 |           1 | pending   | 189.00 | 2026-02-10
--  103 |           2 | shipped   |   9.99 | 2026-02-11
--  104 |           3 | cancelled |  49.00 | 2026-03-01
--  105 |           2 | shipped   | 238.00 | 2026-03-15

-- products: 1 Keyboard 49.00, 2 Mouse 19.50, 3 Monitor 189.00 (hardware),
--           4 Ebook 9.99 (digital)
takeaways: A table holds one kind of thing: each row is one item, each column one fact about it
Every column has a data type; NULL marks a value that is unknown
A primary key identifies each row; tables link by storing those key values
SQL is declarative: say what you want, and the query planner decides how
pitfalls: Assuming rows come back in the order they were added. Unless you ask for a sort, the order is not guaranteed and can change between runs.

quiz.q: How does a row in orders record which customer placed it?
options: It keeps a full copy of the customer's name and email
Orders are stored inside the customers table
It stores the customer's id value in its customer_id column
The database remembers which customer was added just before the order
quiz.explain: Tables link through matching values: customer_id holds the id of the related customer.

quiz.q: What does it mean that SQL is declarative?
options: You describe the result you want and the database works out how to get it
You must spell out each step the database takes, in order
Every table must be declared in the same file as the query
Results always come back in the order rows were added
quiz.explain: You state what you want; the query planner decides which table to read first and how to search it.

concepts.name: SELECT: reading data
concepts.summary: Read data from a table with SELECT ... FROM, choosing exactly which columns you want back.
concepts.why: SELECT is the statement you will write most; everything else about querying builds on its shape.
concepts.body:
To read data you write a `SELECT` statement. After `SELECT` you list the columns you want, and after `FROM` you name the table to read them from:

```sql
SELECT name, city FROM customers;
```

The answer comes back as a new table: one row for each customer, with just the two columns you asked for. The part between `SELECT` and `FROM` is called the **select list**. Each part of a statement that starts with a word like `SELECT` or `FROM` is called a **clause**.

`SELECT *` (the star means 'every column') returns all the columns. It's handy for a quick look at a table, but in queries you keep and reuse, name the columns: you get only the data you need, and the result stays the same when someone adds a column to the table later.

Words with a fixed meaning in SQL, such as `SELECT` and `FROM`, are **keywords**. They are not **case-sensitive**: `select` and `SELECT` mean the same. Writing keywords in capitals is just a habit that makes queries easier to read.

A piece of text is called a **string**. When you type one directly into a query, it is a **string literal**, and it goes in single quotation marks: `'London'`.

Double quotation marks mean something else: they wrap an **identifier**, the name of a table or column. You only need them for unusual names, such as a column called `"Order Total"` with a space in it. So in PostgreSQL, `"London"` means 'the column named London', not the text London. (MySQL accepts double-quoted text by default, which confuses people who switch between the two.)

Unquoted names aren't case-sensitive either: PostgreSQL turns them into lower case, so `SELECT Name FROM Customers` finds the table `customers`.

You can also `SELECT` a calculation with no table at all, such as `SELECT 2 + 3;`, which is handy for trying things out. Oracle is the odd one out: it needs `FROM dual` at the end.

One surprise: although you write `SELECT` first, the database deals with `FROM` first. It finds the rows, then filters and groups them, and only at the end builds the select list. Keeping that order in mind explains several rules in later lessons.
concepts.code:
SELECT name, city FROM customers;
--  name  | city
--  Ana   | Yerevan
--  Ben   | London
--  Chloe | London
--  Dev   | NULL

SELECT id, name, price FROM products;
--  id | name     | price
--   1 | Keyboard |  49.00
--   2 | Mouse    |  19.50
--   3 | Monitor  | 189.00
--   4 | Ebook    |   9.99

-- No table needed for a quick calculation
-- (AS names the result column; see the next lesson)
SELECT 2 + 3 AS answer;
--  answer
--       5
takeaways: SELECT columns FROM table returns a new result table
Name the columns you need instead of SELECT * in queries you keep
Single quotation marks for strings, double ones for identifiers
pitfalls: Writing "London" in double quotation marks in PostgreSQL: it is read as a column name and fails with 'column does not exist'.

quiz.q: Why is SELECT * best avoided in queries you keep and reuse?
options: It fetches columns you don't need, and its result changes when someone adds a column to the table
It is not allowed in PostgreSQL
It cannot be used with FROM
It returns rows in random order
quiz.explain: Naming the columns makes it clear what the query needs and keeps its result stable when the table changes.

quiz.q: In PostgreSQL, what does SELECT "London" FROM customers; do?
options: Returns the text London once per customer
Fails, because "London" is read as a column name and there is no such column
Returns the customers who live in London
quiz.explain: Double quotation marks show an identifier, so PostgreSQL looks for a column called London. With single quotation marks, 'London', you would get the text once per row.

concepts.name: Expressions, aliases and DISTINCT
concepts.summary: Calculate new values in a query, name result columns with AS, and remove repeated rows with DISTINCT.
concepts.why: Real questions need calculated values, readable column names and lists without repeats, not just raw columns.
concepts.body:
The select list doesn't have to be plain column names. It can hold any **expression**: a piece of SQL that works out a value, like `price * 1.2` (the star means multiply). Each expression becomes a column of the result:

```sql
SELECT name, price, price * 1.2 AS price_with_vat FROM products;
```

`AS` gives the result column a name, called an **alias**. Without one, PostgreSQL makes up a name such as `?column?`. The word `AS` is optional, but write it anyway. If you forget a comma, `SELECT name city` quietly returns the `name` column labelled `city`; when you always write `AS`, a name without it stands out as a mistake.

Expressions can also use **functions**: named, built-in operations that take values in brackets and give back a result. `upper(name)` gives the name in capitals, and `round(price)` rounds a number. Later lessons introduce many more.

Joining pieces of text end to end is called **concatenation**. PostgreSQL, SQLite and Oracle write it with `||`: `name || ' (' || category || ')'` gives `Keyboard (hardware)`. MySQL and SQL Server use the `concat()` function instead, which PostgreSQL also understands.

Watch out with division. An **integer** is a whole number, like 7 or 2. When you divide one integer by another, PostgreSQL, SQL Server and SQLite throw the fraction away: `7 / 2` gives `3`. This is called **integer division**.

To get `3.5`, make one side a decimal number: write `7 / 2.0`, or convert a column with `CAST(x AS numeric)` (PostgreSQL also accepts the short form `x::numeric`). MySQL is the odd one out and gives `3.5000` either way.

`DISTINCT` removes repeated rows from the result. It looks at the whole row, not just the first column:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers;      -- Yerevan, London, NULL
SELECT DISTINCT city, name FROM customers; -- all 4 rows, each pair is different
```

Removing repeats means the database must compare every result row with the others, which takes time on big results. If you find yourself adding `DISTINCT` to hide rows you didn't expect to see twice, the query itself usually has a mistake.
concepts.code:
SELECT name,
       price,
       price * 1.2               AS price_with_vat,
       name || ' (' || category || ')' AS label
FROM products;
--  name     | price  | price_with_vat | label
--  Keyboard |  49.00 |        58.800 | Keyboard (hardware)
--  Mouse    |  19.50 |        23.400 | Mouse (hardware)
--  Monitor  | 189.00 |       226.800 | Monitor (hardware)
--  Ebook    |   9.99 |        11.988 | Ebook (digital)

SELECT 7 / 2 AS int_div, 7 / 2.0 AS num_div;
--  int_div | num_div
--        3 |  3.5000000000000000

SELECT DISTINCT category FROM products;
--  hardware
--  digital
takeaways: Any expression can appear in the select list; name it with AS
Whole number divided by whole number loses the fraction in PostgreSQL; use 2.0 or CAST for decimals
DISTINCT removes repeated whole rows, not repeated values in one column
pitfalls: Adding DISTINCT to hide unexpected repeated rows instead of finding the mistake in the query that produced them.

quiz.q: What does SELECT DISTINCT city, name FROM customers return for our four customers?
options: 4 rows, because every (city, name) pair is different
An error: DISTINCT accepts only one column
quiz.explain: DISTINCT compares whole result rows, and all four (city, name) combinations are different.

quiz.q: In PostgreSQL, what is SELECT 5 / 2?
quiz.explain: Both numbers are integers, so PostgreSQL does integer division and drops the .5, giving 2.

concepts.name: Filtering rows with WHERE
concepts.summary: Keep only the rows that satisfy a condition, combining comparisons with AND, OR and NOT.
concepts.why: Almost every real query, and every change to data, targets only some rows, chosen with WHERE.
concepts.body:
`WHERE` filters rows. You give it a condition, and only the rows for which the condition is **true** make it into the result:

```sql
SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE status = 'shipped';
```

Conditions compare values using **operators**: symbols that work on values, like `+` or `=`. The comparison operators are `=` (equal), `<>` (not equal; `!=` also works everywhere), `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`. Equality is a single `=`; SQL has no `==`.

Comparing text is exact. In PostgreSQL it also respects capitals: `'london'` does not equal `'London'`. MySQL ignores capitals by default, a common surprise for people who switch between the two.

Combine conditions with `AND` (both must be true), `OR` (at least one must be true) and `NOT` (turns true into false). `AND` is applied before `OR`, just as multiplication comes before addition in arithmetic, so this condition does not do what it seems to say:

```sql
-- shipped orders over 50, OR any order at all from customer 1
WHERE status = 'shipped' AND total > 50 OR customer_id = 1
```

Add parentheses whenever you mix `AND` and `OR`; it costs nothing and removes the doubt.

Because `WHERE` is worked out before the select list, it can't use an alias you created there. Repeat the calculation instead (a later lesson shows another way).

The same `WHERE` clause is used when you change or delete rows, where getting it wrong changes the wrong rows. A good habit: run it as a `SELECT` first, check which rows come back, and only then use it to change data.
concepts.code:
SELECT id, customer_id, total
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'shipped' AND total > 50;
--  id  | customer_id | total
--  101 |           1 |  68.50
--  105 |           2 | 238.00

-- Parentheses make the intent explicit
SELECT id, status
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 1 AND (status = 'pending' OR total < 100);
--  id  | status
--  101 | shipped
--  102 | pending

-- Aliases from SELECT are NOT visible in WHERE:
-- SELECT total * 1.2 AS gross FROM orders WHERE gross > 100;  -- ERROR
SELECT id, total * 1.2 AS gross FROM orders WHERE total * 1.2 > 100;
takeaways: WHERE keeps rows whose condition is true
AND is applied before OR; add parentheses when you mix them
Aliases from the select list cannot be used in WHERE
pitfalls: Forgetting parentheses around an OR, so the filter matches far more rows than intended.

quiz.q: Which rows does WHERE status = 'shipped' OR status = 'pending' AND total > 100 match?
options: Orders that are (shipped or pending) and over 100
All shipped orders, plus pending orders over 100
No rows; the expression is ambiguous and errors
quiz.explain: AND is evaluated first, so the condition reads shipped OR (pending AND total > 100).

quiz.q: Why does SELECT total * 2 AS dbl FROM orders WHERE dbl > 100 fail?
options: Arithmetic is not allowed in WHERE
AS cannot be used with numeric columns
WHERE is evaluated before the select list, so the alias does not exist yet
quiz.explain: Logically FROM and WHERE run before SELECT computes and names its output columns.

concepts.name: IN, BETWEEN and LIKE
concepts.summary: Match against lists, ranges and text patterns with IN, BETWEEN and LIKE.
concepts.why: These operators make common filters shorter and clearer than chains of OR and comparisons.
concepts.body:
Three operators cover most filters that aren't a single comparison.

`IN` tests whether a value is in a list, replacing a chain of `OR`s:

```sql
WHERE status IN ('pending', 'shipped')
```

`NOT IN` is the opposite, but treat it with care: if the list contains a `NULL`, `NOT IN` matches nothing at all. The NULL lesson explains why.

`BETWEEN a AND b` is a range that includes both ends, the same as `>= a AND <= b`. That catches people out with a **timestamp**, a value holding a date plus a time of day. `ordered_at BETWEEN '2026-02-01' AND '2026-02-28'` stops at midnight at the very start of the 28th, so it misses orders placed later that day. For time ranges, include the start and exclude the end instead:

```sql
WHERE ordered_at >= '2026-02-01' AND ordered_at < '2026-03-01'
```

`LIKE` compares text with a **pattern**: a model of the text you want, in which `%` stands for any run of characters (including none) and `_` for exactly one character:

- `name LIKE 'M%'` starts with M
- `email LIKE '%@example.com'` ends with @example.com
- `name LIKE '_o%'` has o as its second letter

In PostgreSQL `LIKE` respects capitals. `ILIKE` is a PostgreSQL-only version that ignores them; elsewhere, convert to lower case first: `lower(name) LIKE 'm%'`. To match a real `%` or `_` character, put a backslash before it: `LIKE '50\%%'` finds text starting with '50%'.

A note on speed. A database can keep an **index** on a column: a sorted list of its values, each pointing to its row, like the index at the back of a book. A pattern with a fixed start, such as `'M%'`, can use it to jump straight to the M's. A pattern that starts with `%`, such as `'%book'`, can't, so the database has to check every row. Indexes get their own lessons later.
concepts.code:
SELECT id, status FROM orders WHERE status IN ('pending', 'cancelled');
--  102 | pending
--  104 | cancelled

SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE price BETWEEN 19.50 AND 49.00;
--  Keyboard | 49.00     <- both ends are included
--  Mouse    | 19.50

SELECT id FROM orders
WHERE ordered_at >= '2026-02-01' AND ordered_at < '2026-03-01';
--  102
--  103

SELECT name FROM products WHERE name LIKE 'M%';
--  Mouse
--  Monitor

SELECT name FROM products WHERE name ILIKE '%BOOK';  -- PostgreSQL only
--  Ebook
takeaways: IN replaces chains of OR; NOT IN breaks if the list contains NULL
BETWEEN includes both ends; use >= and < for time ranges
LIKE: % = any run of characters, _ = exactly one; ILIKE ignores capitals (PostgreSQL only)
pitfalls: Using BETWEEN with a plain date as the upper end on a column that also stores times, and silently losing the last day's rows.

quiz.q: Which names match name LIKE '_o%'?
quiz.explain: _ matches exactly one character, so the second letter must be o: Mouse and Monitor both qualify.

quiz.q: Why is ordered_at >= '2026-02-01' AND ordered_at < '2026-03-01' better than BETWEEN for February?
options: BETWEEN includes its end point, so with a plain date as the end it misses orders later on the last day
BETWEEN does not work with dates
BETWEEN leaves out its end point
quiz.explain: Including the start and excluding the end covers every moment in the month exactly once, whatever the time of day.

concepts.name: NULL and three-valued logic
concepts.summary: NULL means unknown; comparisons with it are neither true nor false, so you test it with IS NULL.
concepts.why: Misunderstanding NULL is the single most common source of silently wrong SQL results.
concepts.body:
`NULL` is not zero, not empty text, and not really a value at all: it marks data that is **unknown** or missing. Dev's `city` is NULL because we don't know it.

Any comparison with an unknown value gives an unknown result. Is Dev's city London? We don't know. Even `NULL = NULL` is not true; it is NULL. So SQL uses **three-valued logic**: a condition is true, false or unknown, and `WHERE` keeps only the rows where it is true. The consequences:

- `WHERE city = NULL` matches nothing. Use `WHERE city IS NULL` or `IS NOT NULL`.
- `WHERE city <> 'London'` does not return Dev, because `NULL <> 'London'` is unknown.
- Arithmetic with NULL gives NULL: `price + NULL` is NULL. So does `'a' || NULL` in PostgreSQL. (Oracle treats empty text `''` as NULL, a notorious difference.)

The nastiest surprise is `NOT IN` with a NULL in the list. `x NOT IN (1, NULL)` means `x <> 1 AND x <> NULL`; the second part is unknown, so the whole condition can never be true and the query returns no rows. It happens most often when the list is produced by another query, such as `WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM ...)`: one NULL `customer_id` and the result is empty. `NOT EXISTS`, covered later, doesn't have this problem.

When you do want 'equal, treating two NULLs as equal', PostgreSQL and the SQL standard offer `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM`: `a IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b` is true when both are NULL.

To use a stand-in when a value is NULL, use the `COALESCE` function: `COALESCE(city, 'unknown')`. It takes several **arguments**, the values inside its brackets, and returns the first one that isn't NULL.

Decide on purpose whether a column may be NULL. If a value is always required, mark the column `NOT NULL` (the lesson on creating tables shows how), and this whole kind of problem disappears.
concepts.code:
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city = NULL;      -- 0 rows!
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city IS NULL;     -- Dev

SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city <> 'London';
--  Ana            <- Dev is missing: NULL <> 'London' is unknown

SELECT name FROM customers
WHERE city IS DISTINCT FROM 'London';
--  Ana
--  Dev

SELECT name, COALESCE(city, 'unknown') AS city FROM customers;
--  Ana   | Yerevan
--  Ben   | London
--  Chloe | London
--  Dev   | unknown

SELECT 1 WHERE 3 NOT IN (1, 2, NULL);              -- 0 rows!
takeaways: NULL means unknown; comparing with it yields unknown, not true or false
Test with IS NULL / IS NOT NULL, never = NULL
NOT IN with any NULL in the list returns no rows
COALESCE supplies a fallback for NULL values
pitfalls: Expecting WHERE col <> 'x' to include rows where col is NULL.

quiz.q: What does SELECT NULL = NULL return?
quiz.explain: Comparing two unknowns gives unknown, which SQL represents as NULL.

quiz.q: orders.customer_id contains a NULL in one row. What does SELECT id FROM customers WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders) return?
quiz.explain: With a NULL in the list, every NOT IN test evaluates to unknown, so no row qualifies.

concepts.name: Sorting and limiting results
concepts.summary: Sort results with ORDER BY, and return only the first rows with LIMIT / FETCH FIRST.
concepts.why: Top-10 lists, results shown a page at a time and anything a person reads need a defined order.
concepts.body:
Without `ORDER BY` the database returns rows in whatever order is quickest for it, and that order can change from one run to the next. If order matters, ask for it:

```sql
SELECT name, price FROM products ORDER BY price DESC;
```

`ASC` (the default) sorts from smallest to largest, `DESC` from largest to smallest. List several columns to break ties: `ORDER BY city, name` sorts by city, then by name within each city. You can also sort by a calculation or by an alias from the select list, because `ORDER BY` is worked out after `SELECT`.

Where NULLs go differs between products. PostgreSQL and Oracle put NULL after every real value, so NULLs come last when sorting `ASC` and first when sorting `DESC`; MySQL, SQLite and SQL Server do the opposite. Say what you want with `NULLS FIRST` or `NULLS LAST` (PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQLite support them).

To get only the first rows, PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite use `LIMIT n`, and `OFFSET m` skips rows before that. The official standard spelling is `FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY`, which PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server accept; older SQL Server code writes `SELECT TOP n`.

Showing results a page at a time, like pages 1, 2 and 3 of search results, is called **pagination**. Two rules for it:

- Make the sort order **unique** before using `LIMIT`. If two rows tie, which comes first is arbitrary, and paging can show a row twice or skip it. Add the primary key as a final tie-breaker: `ORDER BY price DESC, id`.
- `OFFSET 100000` still reads 100,000 rows and throws them away, so deep pages get slow. The faster way is **keyset pagination**: remember the last row you showed and ask for the rows after it, such as `WHERE (price, id) < (49.00, 1) ORDER BY price DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20`. The bracketed pair compares price first and uses id only to break a tie, matching the sort order.
concepts.code:
SELECT name, price FROM products ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 2;
--  Monitor  | 189.00
--  Keyboard |  49.00

-- Standard spelling, same result
SELECT name, price FROM products
ORDER BY price DESC
FETCH FIRST 2 ROWS ONLY;

-- NULLs placed on purpose; id breaks ties so the order never changes
SELECT name, city FROM customers ORDER BY city NULLS FIRST, id;
--  Dev   | NULL
--  Ben   | London
--  Chloe | London
--  Ana   | Yerevan

-- Page 2 of orders, 2 per page, newest first
SELECT id, ordered_at FROM orders
ORDER BY ordered_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 2 OFFSET 2;
--  103 | 2026-02-11
--  102 | 2026-02-10
takeaways: Without ORDER BY, row order is not defined
Make the sort order unique (add the primary key) before using LIMIT
NULL placement differs across products; say NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST
Deep OFFSET is slow; keyset pagination stays fast
pitfalls: Paging with LIMIT and OFFSET over a sort order that isn't unique, so rows repeat or vanish between pages.

quiz.q: In PostgreSQL, where do NULL cities appear in ORDER BY city ASC?
quiz.explain: PostgreSQL sorts NULL after every real value, so ascending order puts NULLs last unless you say NULLS FIRST.

quiz.q: Why can SELECT ... ORDER BY city LIMIT 1 return different customers on different runs?
options: ORDER BY is ignored when LIMIT is present
Ben and Chloe tie on city, and the order among tied rows is not defined
LIMIT always skips the first row
quiz.explain: Rows with equal sort values may come back in any order; add a unique tie-breaker such as id.

concepts.name: Aggregate functions
concepts.summary: Collapse many rows into one value with COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX, and know how they treat NULL.
concepts.why: Counts, totals and averages are the first questions anyone asks of data.
concepts.body:
Often you want one summary number rather than a list: how many orders, the total revenue, the average price. Combining many values into one like this is **aggregation**, and the functions that do it are **aggregate functions**. Without `GROUP BY` (the next lesson), the query returns exactly one row:

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(total), AVG(total) FROM orders WHERE status = 'shipped';
```

The core five are `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG` (average), `MIN` and `MAX`, and they share one rule: **they skip NULLs** (except `COUNT(*)`). That gives three different counts:

- `COUNT(*)` counts rows.
- `COUNT(city)` counts rows where `city` is not NULL.
- `COUNT(DISTINCT city)` counts different non-NULL values.

Skipping NULLs also affects `AVG`: the average of 10, NULL and 20 is 15, not 10. If missing should count as zero, write `AVG(COALESCE(x, 0))`.

Over zero rows, `COUNT` returns 0 but `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN` and `MAX` return NULL, which surprises anyone expecting the sum of nothing to be 0. Wrap it: `COALESCE(SUM(total), 0)`.

The standard `FILTER` clause (PostgreSQL and SQLite) applies a condition to one aggregate only, so a single query can produce several counts at once:

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'shipped') AS shipped,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'pending') AS pending
FROM orders;
```

Other products need a `CASE` expression for this, which a later lesson covers.

Finally, once you aggregate, you can't also select plain columns: `SELECT name, COUNT(*) FROM customers` is an error, because there is one count but four names. To get one result per name or per city, you need `GROUP BY`, the next lesson.
concepts.code:
SELECT COUNT(*)            AS orders,
       SUM(total)          AS revenue,
       ROUND(AVG(total), 2) AS avg_order,
       MAX(total)          AS biggest
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'shipped';
--  orders | revenue | avg_order | biggest
--       3 |  316.49 |    105.50 |  238.00

SELECT COUNT(*) AS customers, COUNT(city) AS with_city,
       COUNT(DISTINCT city) AS cities
FROM customers;
--  customers | with_city | cities
--          4 |         3 |      2

SELECT SUM(total) AS s, COALESCE(SUM(total), 0) AS safe
FROM orders WHERE status = 'refunded';
--  s    | safe
--  NULL |    0
takeaways: Aggregates return one value per group; without GROUP BY, one row total
COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) skips NULLs; other aggregates ignore NULLs too
SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX of zero rows is NULL, not 0
FILTER (WHERE ...) restricts a single aggregate
pitfalls: Reporting COUNT(column) as a row count when the column contains NULLs.

quiz.q: customers has 4 rows and city is NULL for one of them. What is COUNT(city)?
quiz.explain: COUNT(column) skips NULL values, so only the three known cities are counted.

quiz.q: What does SELECT SUM(total) FROM orders WHERE false return?
options: An empty result with no rows
quiz.explain: An aggregate without GROUP BY always returns one row, and SUM over no rows is NULL.

concepts.name: GROUP BY and HAVING
concepts.summary: Aggregate per group with GROUP BY, and filter whole groups with HAVING.
concepts.why: Per-customer totals, per-day counts and per-category averages are all GROUP BY queries.
concepts.body:
`GROUP BY` splits the rows into groups that share the same values in the listed columns, then works out the aggregates once per group:

```sql
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(total) AS spent
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id;
```

The rule that follows: every column in the select list must either be listed in `GROUP BY` or be inside an aggregate. Selecting `status` here would be ambiguous, since one customer has orders with several statuses. PostgreSQL relaxes this slightly: if you group by a table's primary key, you may also select that table's other columns, because the key fixes them. Older MySQL setups let you select anything and quietly return an arbitrary value, which hides mistakes.

`WHERE` and `HAVING` both filter, at different moments:

- `WHERE` filters **rows** before grouping. It can't use aggregates.
- `HAVING` filters **groups** after aggregation, so it can: `HAVING SUM(total) > 200`.

The order in which the database works makes this clear: `FROM`, then `WHERE`, `GROUP BY`, `HAVING`, `SELECT`, `ORDER BY` and finally `LIMIT`. A condition on a plain column belongs in `WHERE`, where it cuts down the work early; put only conditions on aggregates in `HAVING`.

You can group by a calculation too: `date_trunc('month', ordered_at)` cuts each date and time back to the first of its month, which gives monthly figures. NULLs form their own group: all customers with an unknown city land in one group.

A group exists only if at least one row falls into it. A per-customer report built from `orders` alone will never show Dev, who has no orders. Including him means combining the customers and orders tables, which the joins lessons cover.
concepts.code:
SELECT customer_id,
       COUNT(*)   AS orders,
       SUM(total) AS spent
FROM orders
WHERE status <> 'cancelled'          -- row filter, before grouping
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(total) > 200              -- group filter, after aggregation
ORDER BY spent DESC;
--  customer_id | orders | spent
--            1 |      2 | 257.50
--            2 |      2 | 247.99

SELECT date_trunc('month', ordered_at) AS month, COUNT(*)
FROM orders
GROUP BY month
ORDER BY month;
--  2026-01-01 00:00:00+00 | 1
--  2026-02-01 00:00:00+00 | 2
--  2026-03-01 00:00:00+00 | 2
takeaways: Each selected column must be grouped or inside an aggregate
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after
Order of work: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT
Groups only exist for values present in the data
pitfalls: Putting non-aggregate conditions in HAVING instead of WHERE, which works but filters late and reads oddly.
Expecting groups with zero rows to appear in the result.

quiz.q: Where must the condition 'only customers who spent more than 200 in total' go?
quiz.explain: It depends on an aggregate over each group, so it can only be evaluated by HAVING after grouping.

quiz.q: Why is SELECT customer_id, status, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id rejected?
options: status is neither grouped nor aggregated, so its value per group is ambiguous
COUNT(*) cannot be used with GROUP BY
GROUP BY must list every column of the table
quiz.explain: A customer can have orders with different statuses, so the query does not say which one to show.

concepts.name: Creating and altering tables
concepts.summary: Define tables with CREATE TABLE, change them with ALTER TABLE, and delete them when they are no longer needed.
concepts.why: Before you can store data you need a table, and the design of real databases changes over time.
concepts.body:
`CREATE TABLE` makes a new table. It names the table and lists its columns, each with a data type and optional extras:

```sql
CREATE TABLE products (
    id       bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    name     text          NOT NULL,
    category text          NOT NULL DEFAULT 'hardware',
    price    numeric(10,2) NOT NULL
);
```

`text` and `numeric(10,2)` are data types: text of any length, and a number with up to 10 digits, 2 of them after the decimal point. The next lesson covers types.

Most of the extras are **constraints**: rules the database checks on every change, rejecting anything that breaks them. A later lesson covers more of them.

- `NOT NULL` forbids missing values. Make it your default, and allow NULL only when 'unknown' is a real possibility.
- `DEFAULT` gives the value to use when a new row doesn't provide one.
- `PRIMARY KEY` marks the identifying column, and `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` makes the database number new rows 1, 2, 3 by itself. A later lesson covers both.

Name tables and columns in lower case, with underscores between words (`order_items`, `customer_id`). If you create a name in double quotation marks with capitals, like `"OrderItems"`, you must type it that way, marks and capitals included, forever after.

Tables change over time, and `ALTER TABLE` changes one in place: add or drop a column, rename one, change its type, add a rule. Statements that create or change the structure of a database, such as `CREATE`, `ALTER` and `DROP`, are known as **DDL** (data definition language).

A planned change to the structure of a database that is already in use is called a **migration**. On a big table that an app is using, some changes are instant and some are not. Adding a column that allows NULL is quick in PostgreSQL. Changing a column's type usually makes the database rewrite the whole table.

While it rewrites, the database holds a **lock** on the table: a claim that stops others from using it in ways that would clash. Other queries that need the table wait until the change finishes, which on a large table can mean minutes.

`DROP TABLE` deletes a table and all its data permanently. `IF EXISTS` and `IF NOT EXISTS` skip the statement when there is nothing to do, so a file of setup statements can safely be run twice.
takeaways: CREATE TABLE lists columns with types, NOT NULL, DEFAULT and keys
ALTER TABLE changes a table in place; some changes rewrite and lock it
`DROP TABLE` deletes the table and its data for good
pitfalls: Creating names with capitals inside double quotation marks, like "CustomerId", and then having to type them exactly that way in every query.

quiz.q: A table was created with CREATE TABLE "OrderItems" (...). Which query works in PostgreSQL?
quiz.explain: Quoted names keep their capitals, and unquoted names are turned into lower case, so only the quoted form matches.

quiz.q: A new row is added without a value for created_at, which is declared NOT NULL DEFAULT now(). What does created_at get?
quiz.explain: DEFAULT supplies the value whenever a new row doesn't provide one; now() is the current date and time.

concepts.name: Choosing data types
concepts.summary: Pick the right type for whole numbers, money, text, true/false values and dates, and avoid the classic mistakes.
concepts.why: Types stop wrong values getting in, decide how much space data takes, and decide how comparisons and arithmetic behave.
concepts.body:
Every column has a data type, and choosing well prevents a whole category of mistakes. Here are the PostgreSQL types you'll use most, one group at a time.

**Whole numbers.** An **integer** is a whole number such as 42 or -7. Computer storage is measured in **bytes**. The `integer` type uses 4 bytes and holds values up to about 2.1 billion either side of zero; `bigint` uses 8 bytes and holds far more. Use `bigint` for ids of tables that may grow: running out of `integer` ids on a busy table is a painful fix.

**Exact decimals.** `numeric(p, s)` stores numbers exactly, with `p` digits in total and `s` of them after the point; `numeric(10,2)` suits prices. Use it for money.

**Approximate decimals.** `real` and `double precision` store **floating-point numbers**: fast, but approximate, so `0.1 + 0.2` is not exactly `0.3`. Fine for measurements such as temperatures, wrong for money.

**Text.** `text` holds text of any length; `varchar(n)` is the same but rejects anything longer than `n` characters. In PostgreSQL they are equally fast. Avoid `char(n)`, which pads short values with spaces.

**True or false.** A **boolean** column holds `true` or `false` (or NULL). MySQL has no real boolean type and uses a tiny number instead; SQL Server uses `bit`.

**Dates and times.** `date` holds a calendar day. A **timestamp** holds a date plus a time of day. Prefer `timestamptz` over plain `timestamp`, which ignores the **time zone**: the local clock of a region, such as London's or Yerevan's.

`timestamptz` stores the exact moment in **UTC**, the world's standard clock, and shows it in the time zone your connection uses. So an order placed at 9:00 in Yerevan and one placed at 9:00 in London are stored as the different moments they are.

**Ids and more.** `uuid` holds long random ids that are unique everywhere; `jsonb` and other types come in later lessons.

Convert between types with `CAST(x AS type)` or PostgreSQL's short form `x::type`. Text in quotation marks, such as `'2026-03-01'`, takes its type from where it's used, which is why comparing it to a `date` column just works.

Products differ more here than anywhere else. SQLite will store text in a number column without complaint. Oracle uses `NUMBER` and `VARCHAR2`, and treats empty text as NULL. MySQL's `DATETIME` has no time zone.
concepts.code:
CREATE TABLE orders (
    id          bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id bigint        NOT NULL,
    status      text          NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
    total       numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,     -- exact: money
    is_gift     boolean       NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
    ordered_at  timestamptz   NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- float8 is short for double precision
SELECT 0.1::float8 + 0.2::float8 = 0.3::float8;    -- false
SELECT 0.1::numeric + 0.2::numeric = 0.3;          -- true

SELECT CAST('42' AS integer) + 1;                  -- 43
SELECT '2026-03-01'::date + 30;                    -- 2026-03-31

-- pg_typeof shows the type of a value
SELECT pg_typeof(total), pg_typeof(ordered_at) FROM orders LIMIT 1;
--  numeric | timestamp with time zone
takeaways: Use numeric for money, never a floating-point type
Default to bigint ids and timestamptz for moments in time
text and varchar(n) perform the same in PostgreSQL
Convert types with CAST(x AS type) or x::type
pitfalls: Storing prices in double precision and getting rounding errors in totals.
Using timestamp without time zone for events from users in different zones.

quiz.q: Which type should store an order total of 19.99?
quiz.explain: numeric stores decimal values exactly; floating-point types store 19.99 only approximately.

quiz.q: In PostgreSQL, what is the practical difference between text and varchar(100)?
options: varchar(100) only adds a maximum-length check
quiz.explain: Both are stored the same way; the length limit is just a rule the database checks.

concepts.name: INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE
concepts.summary: Add rows with INSERT, change them with UPDATE, remove them with DELETE, and see the affected rows with RETURNING.
concepts.why: Reading data is half the job; apps constantly add, change and remove rows.
concepts.body:
`INSERT` adds rows. Always list the columns you're filling, so the statement doesn't depend on the order of the table's columns, and the columns you leave out get their defaults:

```sql
INSERT INTO customers (name, email, city)
VALUES ('Eve', 'eve@example.com', 'Paris'),
       ('Finn', 'finn@example.com', NULL);
```

One statement with several `VALUES` rows is much faster than many one-row statements. `INSERT INTO t (...) SELECT ...` copies in the result of a query instead.

`UPDATE` changes columns of the rows that match `WHERE`. The new value can be worked out from the old one:

```sql
UPDATE products SET price = price * 1.10 WHERE category = 'hardware';
```

`DELETE` removes the matching rows:

```sql
DELETE FROM orders WHERE status = 'cancelled';
```

The rule that saves careers: **an UPDATE or DELETE without WHERE changes every row**. Run the matching `SELECT` first.

When you change data by hand, also use a **transaction**: a group of statements that are kept or undone together. `BEGIN` starts one. Your changes are then provisional until you finish with `COMMIT`, which keeps them (you **commit** the transaction), or `ROLLBACK`, which undoes them all. A **rollback** is your undo button, as long as you haven't committed.

`RETURNING` (PostgreSQL and SQLite; SQL Server's version is `OUTPUT`) hands back the rows you just changed. You see the id the database generated, or the new values, without running a second query. MySQL has no `RETURNING`; use `LAST_INSERT_ID()` there.

To empty a whole table, `TRUNCATE orders` is much faster than `DELETE FROM orders`, because it doesn't go through the rows one by one. It takes a stronger lock on the table while it runs, and in PostgreSQL it can still be undone with `ROLLBACK`.

Every statement reports how many rows it affected (`UPDATE 3` in psql). If an app's update matched zero rows, that is often a sign something is wrong.
concepts.code:
INSERT INTO customers (name, email, city)
VALUES ('Eve', 'eve@example.com', 'Paris')
RETURNING id, name;
--  id | name
--   5 | Eve

UPDATE products
SET price = price * 1.10
WHERE category = 'hardware'
RETURNING name, price;
--  Keyboard |  53.90
--  Mouse    |  21.45
--  Monitor  | 207.90

BEGIN;
DELETE FROM orders WHERE status = 'cancelled';   -- DELETE 1
-- looks right? COMMIT; otherwise:
ROLLBACK;
takeaways: Always list the columns in INSERT
UPDATE and DELETE without WHERE affect every row
BEGIN ... COMMIT or ROLLBACK lets you check changes before keeping them
RETURNING gives you generated ids and new values without a second query
pitfalls: Highlighting only part of an UPDATE in a database app and running it without its WHERE line, which changes every row.

quiz.q: What does UPDATE products SET price = 0; do?
options: Sets the price of every product to 0
Does nothing until COMMIT in every database
quiz.explain: With no WHERE clause, every row matches the update.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of INSERT ... RETURNING id?
options: It checks that the new row is valid
It undoes the insert automatically if something fails
It gives back the generated id without a second query
quiz.explain: RETURNING sends back values from the inserted rows, including ones the database generated.

concepts.name: Primary keys and identity columns
concepts.summary: Identify every row with a primary key, usually a number or a UUID that the database generates.
concepts.why: Keys are what updates, deletes and links between tables use to find exactly one row.
concepts.body:
A **primary key** is a column, or set of columns, whose value identifies one row. Declaring one gives you three things at once: values must be unique, they may not be NULL, and the database builds an **index** on it. An index is a sorted lookup list of the key's values, like the index at the back of a book; it lets the database check uniqueness quickly and makes finding a row by its key fast. A table has at most one primary key.

There are two schools of key.

A **natural key** is real-world data, like a book's ISBN or a country code. Tempting, but real-world values change and get reused more often than anyone expects.

A **surrogate key** is a meaningless id the database makes up. It never needs to change, which is why most tables use one, plus a `UNIQUE` rule on the real-world value (such as `email`) so that stays unique too.

For generated number ids, the standard way to write it is an **identity column**, supported by PostgreSQL 10+ and Oracle 12c+. `GENERATED ALWAYS` rejects ids you try to supply yourself; `GENERATED BY DEFAULT` allows them. Older PostgreSQL code uses `serial`, which does the same job less cleanly. MySQL writes `AUTO_INCREMENT`; SQL Server writes `IDENTITY(1,1)`.

The numbers come from a sequence: a counter inside the database that hands out the next value. A number taken by an insert that then fails or is undone is never handed back, so ids can have gaps. Never rely on them being consecutive.

A `uuid` key is a long random id that can be created anywhere, even in an app before it talks to the database, without asking the database for the next number. A **UUID** also doesn't reveal how many rows you have. The cost: 16 bytes instead of 8, and random values land in scattered places in the index, which slows inserts on big tables. Newer time-ordered UUIDs (version 7) avoid most of that.

A key can span several columns, called a **composite key**. A line in `order_items` is identified by the order and the product together: `PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)`.
concepts.code:
CREATE TABLE customers (
    id    bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    name  text NOT NULL,
    email text NOT NULL UNIQUE          -- natural attribute stays unique
);

CREATE TABLE order_items (
    order_id   bigint  NOT NULL,
    product_id bigint  NOT NULL,
    quantity   integer NOT NULL,
    unit_price numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)  -- composite key
);

INSERT INTO customers (name, email) VALUES ('Ana', 'ana@example.com')
RETURNING id;                           -- 1

INSERT INTO customers (id, name, email) VALUES (99, 'X', 'x@example.com');
-- ERROR: cannot insert a non-DEFAULT value into column "id"
--        (column is GENERATED ALWAYS)
takeaways: A primary key is unique, NOT NULL and automatically indexed
Prefer surrogate keys, plus UNIQUE rules on real-world values
Use GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY (standard) rather than serial
Generated ids can have gaps; never depend on them being consecutive
pitfalls: Using a changeable natural value, such as an email address, as the primary key referenced by other tables.

quiz.q: Which guarantee does a PRIMARY KEY give that a plain UNIQUE rule does not?
quiz.explain: Both are unique and indexed, but a primary key also forbids NULL; UNIQUE allows NULLs.

quiz.q: After a failed insert, the next identity value skips a number. Why?
options: The sequence hands out each number once and never takes it back, even when the insert fails
The primary key index was rebuilt
quiz.explain: Sequence numbers are not returned on failure, so gaps are normal and expected.

concepts.name: Foreign keys and referential integrity
concepts.summary: Use foreign keys so the database guarantees that every link between tables points at a row that really exists.
concepts.why: Without them, orders for customers who no longer exist creep in, and reports quietly lose or invent data.
concepts.body:
A **foreign key** declares that a column's values must exist in another table's key column. With

```sql
customer_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES customers (id)
```

the database rejects an order for a customer that doesn't exist, and rejects deleting a customer who still has orders.

That guarantee is called **referential integrity**. The database enforces it on every change, from every app and every person, forever. Checks written in an app can't match it: two people saving changes at the same moment, or someone fixing data by hand, slip past them. Rows whose link points at nothing are called orphaned rows.

What happens when the referenced row is deleted, or its key changes, is set with `ON DELETE` / `ON UPDATE`:

- `NO ACTION` / `RESTRICT` (the default behaviour): refuse the delete while links to it exist.
- `CASCADE`: delete the linked rows too. Right for rows that belong to their parent, such as the `order_items` of an order; dangerous for anything with value of its own.
- `SET NULL` / `SET DEFAULT`: keep the linked row and clear its link.

The referenced column must be a primary key or have a `UNIQUE` rule. The referencing column, however, is **not** indexed automatically in PostgreSQL (MySQL does create one). Without that index, deleting a customer forces a read of the whole `orders` table to look for links, and looking up a customer's orders is slow. Index foreign-key columns as a rule.

Foreign keys are also documentation: anyone reading the schema, and many tools, can see how tables connect.

When loading data in bulk where rows point at each other in an awkward order, PostgreSQL lets a foreign key be `DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED`. It is then checked once, at the end of the whole **transaction** (the group of statements being saved together), instead of after every statement.
concepts.code:
CREATE TABLE orders (
    id          bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES customers (id),
    status      text   NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
    total       numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
    ordered_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id);    -- not created automatically

CREATE TABLE order_items (
    order_id   bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES orders (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    product_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES products (id),
    quantity   integer NOT NULL,
    unit_price numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)
);

INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, total) VALUES (999, 10);
-- ERROR: insert or update on table "orders" violates foreign key
--        constraint "orders_customer_id_fkey"

DELETE FROM orders WHERE id = 104;   -- its order_items go too (CASCADE)
DELETE FROM customers WHERE id = 1;  -- ERROR: still referenced from orders
takeaways: A foreign key guarantees every link points at an existing row
ON DELETE CASCADE for rows owned by their parent, RESTRICT/NO ACTION otherwise
PostgreSQL does not index the referencing column; add the index yourself
pitfalls: Relying on app code instead of foreign keys, then finding orphaned rows months later.
Putting ON DELETE CASCADE on links to valuable data, so one delete wipes out history.

quiz.q: order_items.order_id references orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE. What does deleting order 101 do?
options: Deletes the order and sets order_items.order_id to NULL
Deletes the order and its order_items rows
quiz.explain: CASCADE propagates the delete to every referencing row.

quiz.q: Why should you usually create an index on orders.customer_id in PostgreSQL?
options: Foreign keys cannot be created without one
PostgreSQL does not create it automatically, and deletes on customers and joins need it
It makes the column NOT NULL
It is required for ON DELETE CASCADE syntax
quiz.explain: Only the referenced side is indexed by its key; the referencing side needs an explicit index.

concepts.name: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK and DEFAULT
concepts.summary: Write business rules into the table definition with NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK and DEFAULT.
concepts.why: Constraints stop bad data at the door, no matter which app or person writes it.
concepts.body:
A constraint is a rule attached to a table that turns an assumption into a guarantee. The database checks it on every insert and update, and rejects the statement if it fails.

- `NOT NULL`: the column must have a value.
- `UNIQUE`: no two rows share the value (or the combination, for `UNIQUE (a, b)`). The database checks it with a unique index.
- `CHECK (expression)`: every row must satisfy the condition, such as `price >= 0` or `status IN ('pending', 'shipped', 'cancelled')`. A check may compare several columns of the same row, but can't look at other rows or tables.
- `DEFAULT`: not a restriction, but written alongside them: the value used when an insert leaves the column out.

Two NULL subtleties matter. First, `UNIQUE` treats NULLs as different from each other, so many rows may have a NULL email. PostgreSQL 15 added `UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT` for the other behaviour; SQL Server, unusually, allows only one NULL. Second, a `CHECK` passes when its condition is NULL. `CHECK (price > 0)` accepts a NULL price; add `NOT NULL` if the value is required.

Name your constraints (`CONSTRAINT price_positive CHECK (...)`). The name appears in error messages, which makes failures readable, and you need it to remove the constraint later.

Adding a constraint to a big existing table means checking every row while holding a lock that blocks changes. PostgreSQL lets you split that: `ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID` applies the rule to new changes straight away, and a later `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` checks the old rows with a much weaker lock.

A note on MySQL: before version 8.0.16 it accepted `CHECK` constraints and then silently ignored them. Don't assume an old MySQL schema enforces what it declares.
concepts.code:
CREATE TABLE products (
    id       bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    sku      text NOT NULL,
    name     text NOT NULL,
    category text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'hardware',
    price    numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT products_sku_key  UNIQUE (sku),
    CONSTRAINT price_non_negative CHECK (price >= 0),
    CONSTRAINT category_known
        CHECK (category IN ('hardware', 'digital'))
);

INSERT INTO products (sku, name, price) VALUES ('KB-1', 'Keyboard', -5);
-- ERROR: new row for relation "products" violates check constraint
--        "price_non_negative"

-- Add a rule to a large table without a long lock
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT total_non_negative
    CHECK (total >= 0) NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT total_non_negative;
takeaways: Constraints are enforced for every writer, unlike checks in app code
UNIQUE allows several NULLs; CHECK passes when its condition is NULL
Name constraints so error messages are readable
`NOT VALID` plus `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` adds a rule to a big table safely
pitfalls: Writing CHECK (price > 0) and assuming it also forbids a NULL price.

quiz.q: A table has email text UNIQUE (nullable). Can two rows have a NULL email in PostgreSQL by default?
options: Yes, NULLs are treated as distinct from each other
No, UNIQUE forbids duplicates including NULL
Only if the table has no primary key
quiz.explain: By default NULLs never equal each other, so they do not violate UNIQUE; NULLS NOT DISTINCT changes this.

quiz.q: Which rule can a CHECK constraint express?
options: The customer referenced by an order must exist
No two products may share a name
An order's discount must not exceed its total
A customer may have at most five orders
quiz.explain: CHECK compares columns within one row; the others need other rows or tables (foreign key, UNIQUE, triggers).

concepts.name: Inner joins
concepts.summary: Combine rows from several tables by matching key values with JOIN ... ON.
concepts.why: Well-designed databases spread data over many tables; joins put it back together to answer real questions.
concepts.body:
A **join** pairs rows from two tables according to a condition. The most common form, the **inner join**, keeps only the pairs where the condition is true:

```sql
SELECT o.id, c.name, o.total
FROM orders AS o
JOIN customers AS c ON c.id = o.customer_id;
```

`JOIN` means `INNER JOIN`. `orders AS o` gives the table a short alias, `o`. Aliases save typing, and become necessary as soon as two tables share column names such as `id` or `name`. Write every column with its table's alias (`o.total`, not just `total`): it keeps the query readable, and stops it breaking when someone adds a same-named column to the other table.

Think of a join as: for each order, find the customer rows that satisfy `ON`. One customer can have many orders, a **one-to-many** relationship, so the customer's columns repeat once per order. Joins **multiply** rows: a row matching three rows on the other side appears three times.

That's exactly right for orders and customers, and it's the cause of most 'my totals are too big' mistakes. Join two separate one-to-many tables (say, order items and payments) to the same order and then `SUM`, and every item is counted once per payment.

Chaining joins walks the schema. To list what each customer bought: `customers` to `orders` to `order_items` to `products`.

When the join columns have the same name on both sides, `USING (order_id)` is a shorter `ON`. A table can also be joined to itself under two different aliases, a **self join**, for example to pair customers from the same city. `CROSS JOIN` returns every combination of rows with no condition: useful for building grids, alarming when it happens by accident.

Older code writes joins as `FROM a, b WHERE a.id = b.a_id`. It means the same, but `JOIN ... ON` keeps the join conditions apart from the filters and makes a forgotten condition obvious.
concepts.code:
SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id, p.name AS product, oi.quantity
FROM customers   AS c
JOIN orders      AS o  ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id   = o.id
JOIN products    AS p  ON p.id          = oi.product_id
WHERE o.status = 'shipped'
ORDER BY o.id, p.name;
--  name | order_id | product  | quantity
--  Ana  |      101 | Keyboard |        1
--  Ana  |      101 | Mouse    |        1
--  Ben  |      103 | Ebook    |        1
--  Ben  |      105 | Keyboard |        1
--  Ben  |      105 | Monitor  |        1

-- Self join: pairs of customers in the same city
SELECT a.name, b.name
FROM customers a
JOIN customers b ON b.city = a.city AND a.id < b.id;
--  Ben | Chloe
takeaways: JOIN ... ON keeps the pairs of rows where the condition is true
Give tables aliases and prefix every column with one
Joins multiply rows: one-to-many repeats the 'one' side
Prefer JOIN ... ON over the old comma style
pitfalls: Joining two unrelated one-to-many tables to the same parent and summing, which inflates totals.

quiz.q: Ana has 2 orders, Ben 2, Chloe 1, Dev 0. How many rows does customers JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = customers.id return?
quiz.explain: An inner join returns one row per matching pair: 5 orders, each matched to one customer; Dev has no match.

quiz.q: Why is a.id < b.id included in the self join of customers by city?
options: To make the join use an index
Because self joins require an inequality
To drop pairs of a customer with themselves and avoid each pair appearing twice
quiz.explain: Without it, every customer pairs with itself and (Ben, Chloe) also appears as (Chloe, Ben).

concepts.name: Outer joins: LEFT, RIGHT and FULL
concepts.summary: Keep rows without a match using LEFT, RIGHT and FULL joins, and find unmatched rows.
concepts.why: Reports must include customers with no orders and products never sold; inner joins silently drop them.
concepts.body:
An inner join drops rows that have no partner. Dev has no orders, so he disappears from any customers-orders inner join. An **outer join** keeps them:

```sql
SELECT c.name, o.id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;
```

`LEFT JOIN` keeps every row of the left (first) table. Where there is no match, the right table's columns are filled with NULL. `RIGHT JOIN` is the mirror image (rarely used; swap the tables and write a LEFT JOIN instead), and `FULL JOIN` keeps unmatched rows from both sides. MySQL has no `FULL JOIN`.

Those NULLs make outer joins useful for finding what's missing, a technique called an **anti-join**:

```sql
SELECT c.name FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;          -- Dev
```

Two classic mistakes:

- **Filtering the right table in WHERE.** `LEFT JOIN orders o ... WHERE o.status = 'shipped'` removes the NULL-filled rows (NULL is not 'shipped'), quietly turning the query back into an inner join. A condition about the optional side belongs in `ON`: `LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'shipped'`.
- **Counting with COUNT(*).** For Dev, the left join produces one row with NULL order columns, so `COUNT(*)` says 1. Count a column from the right table, `COUNT(o.id)`, which skips NULLs and gives 0.

When a result looks odd, ask of each table: must a match exist (inner join), or is it optional (outer join)?
concepts.code:
SELECT c.name,
       COUNT(o.id)                  AS orders,   -- not COUNT(*)
       COALESCE(SUM(o.total), 0)    AS spent
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
       ON o.customer_id = c.id
      AND o.status <> 'cancelled'               -- optional side: filter in ON
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY spent DESC;
--  name  | orders | spent
--  Ana   |      2 | 257.50
--  Ben   |      2 | 247.99
--  Chloe |      0 |   0
--  Dev   |      0 |   0

-- Products never ordered (anti-join)
SELECT p.name
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id
WHERE oi.product_id IS NULL;
--  (no rows: every product has been ordered)
takeaways: LEFT JOIN keeps all left rows, NULL-filling missing matches
WHERE right_col IS NULL after a LEFT JOIN finds unmatched rows
Conditions on the optional table go in ON, not WHERE
Count a right-side column, not *, to get zero for no matches
pitfalls: A WHERE condition on the right table that turns a LEFT JOIN into an inner join.

quiz.q: customers LEFT JOIN orders ... WHERE o.status = 'shipped'. Does Dev (no orders) appear?
options: Yes, but only if status allows NULL
No, because NULL = 'shipped' is not true, so WHERE removes his row
It depends on the join order the planner picks
quiz.explain: WHERE runs after the join and drops the NULL-extended row; move the condition into ON to keep him.

quiz.q: For a customer with no orders, what does COUNT(*) return in a customers LEFT JOIN orders GROUP BY customer query?
quiz.explain: The outer join produces one row for that customer, and COUNT(*) counts it; COUNT(o.id) would give 0.

concepts.name: Subqueries and EXISTS
concepts.summary: Nest one query inside another as a single value, a list, a temporary table or an EXISTS test.
concepts.why: Many questions are easiest to express as 'rows where something about other rows is true'.
concepts.body:
A **subquery** is a `SELECT` in parentheses used inside another statement. Where it appears decides what it must return.

A **scalar subquery** returns exactly one value (one row, one column) and can go wherever a single value can:

```sql
SELECT name, price FROM products
WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products);
```

A subquery after `IN` returns one column, used as a list: `WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending')`.

A **derived table** is a subquery in `FROM`, used like a temporary table. It lets you work further on a grouped result, for example averaging per-customer totals. Most databases require an alias for it; PostgreSQL made the alias optional in version 16.

`EXISTS (subquery)` is true when the subquery returns at least one row. It usually refers to the outer row, which makes it a **correlated subquery**:

```sql
SELECT c.name FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);
```

In principle it runs once per outer row, though the query planner usually turns it into a join that keeps each customer only once, a **semi-join**. What you select inside doesn't matter; `SELECT 1` is the convention.
