Prefer `NOT EXISTS` to `NOT IN` for 'rows with no match'. `NOT IN` returns nothing at all if the subquery produces a single NULL, whereas `NOT EXISTS` behaves as you expect and runs as an efficient anti-join.

Subqueries or joins? If you need columns from the other table, join. If you only need to know whether related rows exist, `EXISTS` states the intent and never repeats outer rows, which a join to a one-to-many table would.
concepts.code:
-- Scalar subquery
SELECT name, price FROM products
WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products);    -- avg = 66.87
--  Monitor | 189.00

-- Semi-join: customers with at least one shipped order (no duplicates)
SELECT c.name FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o
              WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'shipped');
--  Ana
--  Ben

-- Anti-join: customers with no orders, NULL-safe
SELECT c.name FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);
--  Dev

-- Derived table: average spend per ordering customer
SELECT ROUND(AVG(spent), 2) AS avg_spent
FROM (SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS spent
      FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) AS per_customer;
--  184.83
takeaways: Scalar subqueries return one value; IN subqueries return one column
A subquery in FROM is a derived table
EXISTS tests for related rows without duplicating outer rows
Use NOT EXISTS, not NOT IN, for 'no matching rows'
pitfalls: A scalar subquery that can return more than one row: it works today and fails later, when the data changes.

quiz.q: Why might a join to orders return Ana twice while WHERE EXISTS (...) returns her once?
options: EXISTS removes duplicates with an implicit DISTINCT
EXISTS only checks the first order
A join produces one row per matching order; EXISTS only asks whether any match exists
quiz.explain: EXISTS is a yes/no test per outer row, while a join pairs the outer row with each match.

quiz.q: What does a correlated subquery refer to?
options: A column of the outer query's current row
quiz.explain: Correlation means the inner query uses values from the row the outer query is evaluating.

concepts.name: CASE, COALESCE and NULLIF
concepts.summary: Write if-then logic inside queries with CASE, and handle NULLs with COALESCE and NULLIF.
concepts.why: Sorting values into buckets, labelling, turning rows into columns and safe division all need if-then logic inside SQL.
concepts.body:
`CASE` is SQL's if-then-else. It produces a value, so it can appear anywhere an expression can: in `SELECT`, `WHERE`, `ORDER BY`, even inside aggregate functions.

The **searched** form tests conditions in order and returns the first match:

```sql
CASE
    WHEN total >= 100 THEN 'large'
    WHEN total >= 20  THEN 'medium'
    ELSE 'small'
END
```

The **simple** form compares one expression with values: `CASE status WHEN 'shipped' THEN 1 WHEN 'pending' THEN 2 ELSE 3 END`. Without `ELSE`, unmatched rows get NULL. All the results must be of compatible types (all numbers, or all text).

Inside an aggregate, `CASE` lets one query compute several totals, each for a different condition. That is the portable way to **pivot**: turn values spread over rows into separate columns.

```sql
SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'shipped' THEN total ELSE 0 END) AS shipped_value
```

Two shorthands handle NULL:

- `COALESCE(a, b, c)` returns the first argument that isn't NULL. Use it for defaults: `COALESCE(city, 'unknown')`. It is standard; `IFNULL` (MySQL, SQLite), `ISNULL` (SQL Server) and `NVL` (Oracle) are two-argument versions specific to those products.
- `NULLIF(a, b)` returns NULL if `a = b`, otherwise `a`. Its classic use is avoiding division by zero: `x / NULLIF(y, 0)` gives NULL instead of an error.

PostgreSQL, MySQL and Oracle also have `GREATEST` and `LEAST` for the largest or smallest of several values. In PostgreSQL they ignore NULL arguments, while in MySQL and Oracle any NULL makes the result NULL.

`CASE` stops at the first true `WHEN`, so put the narrower conditions first.
concepts.code:
SELECT id, total,
       CASE WHEN total >= 100 THEN 'large'
            WHEN total >= 20  THEN 'medium'
            ELSE 'small'
       END AS size
FROM orders ORDER BY id;
--  101 |  68.50 | medium
--  102 | 189.00 | large
--  103 |   9.99 | small
--  104 |  49.00 | medium
--  105 | 238.00 | large

-- Pivot: one row per customer, a column per status
SELECT customer_id,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'shipped' THEN total ELSE 0 END) AS shipped,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'pending' THEN total ELSE 0 END) AS pending
FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id;
--  1 |  68.50 | 189.00
--  2 | 247.99 |   0
--  3 |   0    |   0

SELECT 10 / NULLIF(0, 0) AS safe_div;   -- NULL, not a division error
takeaways: CASE returns the value of the first true WHEN, else ELSE (or NULL)
CASE inside SUM/COUNT pivots rows into columns
COALESCE supplies defaults; NULLIF(y, 0) prevents division by zero
pitfalls: Omitting ELSE and being surprised by NULLs in the result.

quiz.q: What does CASE WHEN total > 10 THEN 'a' WHEN total > 100 THEN 'b' END give for total = 238?
quiz.explain: WHEN clauses are tested in order and the first true one wins, so 'a' is returned.

quiz.q: What does COALESCE(NULL, NULL, 'x', 'y') return?
quiz.explain: COALESCE returns its first non-NULL argument.

concepts.name: String functions
concepts.summary: Clean, search, split and join text with SQL's string functions and regular expressions.
concepts.why: Data arrives with stray spaces, mixed capitals and several values crammed into one column; fixing it in SQL saves exporting it to fix elsewhere.
concepts.body:
Every database ships dozens of functions for working with strings. The core set, with PostgreSQL names:

- `length(s)`, `lower(s)`, `upper(s)`.
- `trim(s)` removes spaces at both ends; `ltrim` and `rtrim` remove them from one side.
- `substring(s FROM 2 FOR 3)` or `substr(s, 2, 3)` takes out a **substring**, part of the text; positions start at 1, not 0.
- `position('@' IN email)` finds where a substring starts (0 if it's absent).
- `replace(s, 'from', 'to')` replaces every occurrence.
- `split_part(email, '@', 2)` splits text on a separator and takes the n-th piece.
- `concat_ws(', ', a, b, c)` joins values with a separator and, unlike `||`, skips NULL arguments.
- `left(s, n)`, `right(s, n)`, `lpad(s, n, '0')`.

For anything `LIKE` can't express, PostgreSQL supports **regular expressions**, a mini-language for describing text. `email ~ '^[a-z]+@'` tests whether an email starts with lower-case letters followed by @ (`~*` ignores capitals), and `regexp_replace(phone, '[^0-9]', '', 'g')` removes everything that isn't a digit.

`string_agg(name, ', ' ORDER BY name)` is an aggregate function that joins values from many rows into one string; MySQL calls it `GROUP_CONCAT`, Oracle and the standard `LISTAGG`.

Function names differ between products more than behaviour does. SQL Server uses `LEN` (which ignores trailing spaces) and `CHARINDEX`. MySQL's `LENGTH` counts bytes, the units of storage, not characters. In **UTF-8**, the usual way of storing text, a letter like é takes two bytes, so it counts twice; use `CHAR_LENGTH` there. PostgreSQL's `length` counts characters.

Wrapping a column in a function inside `WHERE`, as in `WHERE lower(email) = 'ana@example.com'`, normally stops the database from using a plain index on `email` (a sorted lookup list of the emails). Either store the data already cleaned up, all in lower case say, or create an index on the expression itself, as the indexing lessons show.
concepts.code:
SELECT email,
       split_part(email, '@', 1)         AS local_part,
       upper(left(name, 1))              AS initial,
       length(name)                      AS len,
       concat_ws(' / ', name, city)      AS label   -- NULL city skipped
FROM customers ORDER BY id;
--  ana@example.com   | ana   | A | 3 | Ana / Yerevan
--  ben@example.com   | ben   | B | 3 | Ben / London
--  chloe@example.com | chloe | C | 5 | Chloe / London
--  dev@example.com   | dev   | D | 3 | Dev

SELECT trim('  Mouse  ') AS t,
       regexp_replace('+1 (555) 010-99', '[^0-9]', '', 'g') AS digits;
--  Mouse | 155501099

SELECT city, string_agg(name, ', ' ORDER BY name) AS people
FROM customers WHERE city IS NOT NULL GROUP BY city ORDER BY city;
--  London  | Ben, Chloe
--  Yerevan | Ana
takeaways: String positions start at 1
concat_ws skips NULLs; || turns the whole result NULL
string_agg (GROUP_CONCAT, LISTAGG) concatenates across rows
Functions on a column in WHERE usually bypass a plain index
pitfalls: Using MySQL's LENGTH on UTF-8 text and getting bytes instead of characters.

quiz.q: In PostgreSQL, what is 'Hi ' || NULL || 'there'?
quiz.explain: The || operator propagates NULL; concat or concat_ws would skip it instead.

quiz.q: Which aggregates names from many rows into one comma-separated string in PostgreSQL?
quiz.explain: string_agg is the aggregate form; concat works on values within a single row.

concepts.name: Dates, times and intervals
concepts.summary: Do date arithmetic, cut timestamps down to days or months, and handle time zones correctly.
concepts.why: Nearly every report is 'per day', 'last 30 days' or 'per month', and time zone mistakes are easy to miss.
concepts.body:
PostgreSQL's date and time support is rich and mostly standard. The building blocks:

- **Current time**: `now()` gives the moment the current transaction started, as a `timestamptz`. `current_date` gives today's date, and `clock_timestamp()` the actual time right now, which keeps moving during a transaction.
- **Intervals**: a length of time, such as `interval '30 days'` or `interval '2 hours'`. Add them to dates and timestamps: `now() - interval '30 days'`. Subtracting two timestamps gives an interval; subtracting two `date`s gives a whole number of days.
- **Truncation**: `date_trunc('month', ordered_at)` rounds down to the start of the month. It is the workhorse of reports grouped by day, week or month.
- **Extraction**: `extract(year FROM ordered_at)`, `extract(dow FROM ...)` (day of week, Sunday = 0), `extract(epoch FROM ...)` (seconds since the start of 1970, a common way to store time as one number).
- **Formatting**: `to_char(ordered_at, 'YYYY-MM-DD')` turns a timestamp into text; `to_date` and `to_timestamp` read text back into dates.

Time zones need care. A `timestamptz` stores an exact moment (internally in UTC) and is displayed in your connection's time zone setting, `TimeZone`. `AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Yerevan'` converts it to the local clock time in that zone.

So 'per day' is ambiguous: whose day? Cut the timestamps to days in the business's own zone, `date_trunc('day', ordered_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/London')`, or orders placed near midnight are counted on the wrong day.

`generate_series(start, stop, interval)` produces one row per step. LEFT JOIN it to your data to fill in the days with no activity, so charts show zeros instead of gaps.

Products differ heavily here: SQL Server uses `DATEADD`, `DATEDIFF` and `GETDATE()`; MySQL uses `DATE_ADD(d, INTERVAL 30 DAY)` and `DATE_FORMAT`. The ideas carry over; the spelling doesn't.
concepts.code:
SELECT now() - interval '30 days'                AS a_month_ago,
       date '2026-03-15' - date '2026-01-05'     AS days_between,  -- 69
       extract(dow FROM date '2026-03-15')       AS weekday;       -- 0 (Sunday)

-- Revenue per month in the shop's time zone
SELECT date_trunc('month', ordered_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/London') AS month,
       SUM(total) AS revenue
FROM orders WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
--  2026-01-01 00:00:00 |  68.50
--  2026-02-01 00:00:00 | 198.99
--  2026-03-01 00:00:00 | 238.00

-- Every day of the week, including days without orders
SELECT d::date AS day, COUNT(o.id) AS orders
FROM generate_series(date '2026-02-09', date '2026-02-15', interval '1 day') AS d
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.ordered_at::date = d::date
GROUP BY d ORDER BY d;
--  2026-02-09 | 0
--  2026-02-10 | 1
--  2026-02-11 | 1
--  2026-02-12 | 0   ...
takeaways: Store moments as timestamptz; convert with AT TIME ZONE for local-day logic
date_trunc cuts timestamps down to a unit; extract pulls out parts
Timestamp arithmetic uses intervals; date minus date gives days
generate_series plus LEFT JOIN fills in days with no data
pitfalls: Grouping by UTC day for a business whose 'day' is in another time zone.

quiz.q: What does date_trunc('month', timestamp '2026-02-11 14:30') return?
quiz.explain: date_trunc rounds down to the start of the given unit, here the first instant of February.

quiz.q: Why might per-day counts differ between a London report and a Yerevan report on the same data?
options: Each day starts at a different instant in each time zone, so orders near midnight fall on different dates
Yerevan does not use the Gregorian calendar
quiz.explain: A calendar day is a time-zone-dependent range of instants.

concepts.name: Views and materialized views
concepts.summary: Save a query under a name with CREATE VIEW, or store its result as a materialized view.
concepts.why: Views give complicated joins a simple name, hide detail from the people using them, and let tables change behind a name that stays the same.
concepts.body:
A **view** is a saved query with a name. You query it like a table, and the database substitutes the saved query each time:

```sql
CREATE VIEW customer_spend AS
SELECT c.id, c.name, COALESCE(SUM(o.total), 0) AS spent
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;
```

A plain view stores no data and always shows current data. It is no faster or slower than the query inside it: the query planner merges the view's definition into your query and optimises the whole thing. Views are useful for:

- giving a well-tested join or calculation one name, instead of copying and pasting it,
- controlling access: you can let a user read a view that shows some columns without letting them read the table,
- keeping an old name working while the tables behind it change.

Simple views over a single table (no `SUM`, `COUNT` or other summaries, no `DISTINCT`, no joins) can be written to in PostgreSQL: `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` on the view go to the table underneath. Add `WITH CHECK OPTION` to refuse changes that would create rows the view itself can't see.

A **materialized view** (PostgreSQL, Oracle; SQL Server has a similar feature called indexed views) runs the query once and stores the result like a table. Reading it is fast, but the data is a frozen copy until you run `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW`.

A normal refresh stops others reading the view until it finishes. `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY` keeps the old data readable meanwhile, but needs a unique index on the materialized view. Use materialized views for expensive summaries where minutes-old data is fine, like dashboards.

`CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` changes a view, but only by adding columns at the end; to rename or remove columns, delete the view and create it again.
concepts.code:
CREATE VIEW customer_spend AS
SELECT c.id, c.name, COALESCE(SUM(o.total), 0) AS spent
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;

SELECT name, spent FROM customer_spend WHERE spent > 100 ORDER BY spent DESC;
--  Ana | 257.50
--  Ben | 247.99

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW monthly_revenue AS
SELECT date_trunc('month', ordered_at) AS month, SUM(total) AS revenue
FROM orders WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY 1;

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON monthly_revenue (month);       -- needed for CONCURRENTLY
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY monthly_revenue;
takeaways: A view is a named query, expanded and optimised each time you use it
Simple single-table views can be written to in PostgreSQL
A materialized view stores results and must be refreshed
`REFRESH ... CONCURRENTLY` needs a unique index but keeps the view readable
pitfalls: Expecting a plain view to store results and speed up an expensive query.

quiz.q: Does querying a plain (non-materialized) view return data as of the last refresh?
options: Only if the view has an index
No, the view's query runs against current data every time
quiz.explain: A plain view stores only its definition; each query runs it again.

quiz.q: What does REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY require?
options: A primary key on the underlying table
A unique index on the materialized view
That no other user is connected
That no rows changed since the last refresh
quiz.explain: The concurrent refresh compares old and new contents row by row, matching them through a unique index.

concepts.name: Index basics
concepts.summary: Speed up lookups, joins and sorting with B-tree indexes, and understand what they cost.
concepts.why: Once a table holds millions of rows, an index is the difference between a 2 ms query and a 20 second one.
concepts.body:
Without an index, finding `orders WHERE customer_id = 2` means reading every row of the table: a **sequential scan**. An index is a separate, sorted copy of a column's values, each pointing to its row, like the index at the back of a book.

The default kind is a **B-tree**. It keeps the values sorted in a shallow tree shape, so the database finds any value in a handful of steps, even among billions of rows. Because it is sorted, it also serves ranges (`<`, `BETWEEN`, `LIKE 'abc%'`) and `ORDER BY` on that column.

```sql
CREATE INDEX orders_customer_id_idx ON orders (customer_id);
```

Primary keys and `UNIQUE` rules create indexes automatically. Foreign-key columns don't, and they are usually the first indexes you should add.

A **multicolumn index** on `(customer_id, ordered_at)` is sorted by `customer_id`, then by `ordered_at` within each customer. It serves `WHERE customer_id = 2`, `WHERE customer_id = 2 AND ordered_at > ...`, and `WHERE customer_id = 2 ORDER BY ordered_at DESC LIMIT 10`. It does not help `WHERE ordered_at > ...` on its own, because the first column isn't narrowed down. Put the columns compared with `=` first and range or sort columns last.

Indexes are not free. Every insert, update and delete must update every index on the table too. Each index also takes space on **disk**, the computer's long-term storage, and busy indexes are kept in **memory**, its faster working storage. Add the indexes your queries need; drop the ones nothing uses.

An index can't help when the query hides the column inside a calculation: `WHERE lower(email) = ...` or `WHERE ordered_at::date = ...` can't use a plain index on that column. And when a condition matches a large share of the table, the query planner rightly picks a sequential scan instead: one straight read beats jumping around for most of the rows.

On a big table that a live app is using, build indexes with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`. It takes longer, but doesn't block changes to the table while it builds.
takeaways: A B-tree index serves equality, ranges and ORDER BY on its columns
PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE create indexes; foreign keys do not
Multicolumn indexes: equality columns first, range/sort columns last
Each index slows writes; wrapping a column in a function bypasses it
pitfalls: Creating an index on (a, b) and expecting it to speed up queries that filter only on b.

quiz.q: Which query can make good use of an index on orders (customer_id, ordered_at)?
quiz.explain: The index is sorted by customer_id first, so it narrows down to one customer and then reads that customer's date range.

quiz.q: Why might the query planner ignore an index on status for WHERE status = 'shipped'?
options: Indexes only work on number columns
If most rows are shipped, reading the whole table in one pass is cheaper
quiz.explain: When a condition matches most rows, jumping through the index row by row costs more than one straight read of the table.

concepts.name: Transactions and ACID
concepts.summary: Group statements with BEGIN, COMMIT and ROLLBACK so they succeed or fail as a unit.
concepts.why: Any change spanning more than one statement, like moving stock or money, is wrong without a transaction.
concepts.body:
A **transaction** groups statements into one all-or-nothing unit. Placing an order means inserting the order, inserting its items and lowering the stock count. If the server crashes halfway, you must not end up with an order and no items.

```sql
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders ...;
INSERT INTO order_items ...;
UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 3;
COMMIT;
```

`COMMIT` makes the changes permanent and visible to others; `ROLLBACK` throws them away. The guarantees are summed up as **ACID**:

- **Atomicity**: all the statements take effect, or none do. An action that can't be left half done is called atomic.
- **Consistency**: rules such as `NOT NULL` and `UNIQUE` hold when you commit.
- **Isolation**: transactions running at the same time, which is called **concurrency**, don't see each other's half-finished work.
- **Durability**: once `COMMIT` returns, the data survives a crash or power cut.

Outside an explicit `BEGIN`, PostgreSQL runs each statement as its own transaction and commits it immediately; this is **autocommit**. Most of the connectors that programs use to talk to PostgreSQL do the same, though some, such as Python's psycopg, start a transaction for you and wait for you to commit.

In PostgreSQL, an error inside a transaction **aborts** it: every later statement fails with 'current transaction is aborted' until you `ROLLBACK`. If you expect a step might fail and want to carry on, set a **savepoint** first: `SAVEPOINT s1;` ... `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s1;` undoes back to that point and keeps the earlier work.

PostgreSQL can even undo structure changes: `CREATE TABLE` and `ALTER TABLE` inside `BEGIN ... ROLLBACK` are rolled back too. MySQL and Oracle commit most such statements immediately, so a half-applied migration stays half-applied.

Keep transactions short. An open transaction holds locks that make other writers wait and, in PostgreSQL, stops the cleanup of old copies of changed rows. Never wait for a person to respond, or for a slow call to another service, while a transaction is open. A connection left 'idle in transaction' (visible in PostgreSQL's `pg_stat_activity` list of connections) is a classic cause of trouble on live systems.
takeaways: BEGIN ... COMMIT makes several statements atomic; ROLLBACK undoes them
ACID: atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability
In PostgreSQL an error aborts the whole transaction unless you use a savepoint
Keep transactions short; never hold one open while waiting on users or networks
pitfalls: Leaving connections 'idle in transaction', which holds locks and stops PostgreSQL cleaning up old row data.

quiz.q: In PostgreSQL, a statement fails inside BEGIN ... and you then run another UPDATE. What happens?
options: The UPDATE fails: the transaction is aborted until ROLLBACK
The earlier statements are automatically committed
quiz.explain: After an error PostgreSQL rejects every command in that transaction until it is rolled back (or rolled back to a savepoint).

quiz.q: Which ACID property guarantees committed data survives a power failure?
quiz.explain: Durability means that once COMMIT returns, the change is safely stored and survives a crash.

concepts.name: Common table expressions (WITH)
concepts.summary: Break a complex query into named steps with WITH, and know when PostgreSQL merges them into the main query or computes them separately.
concepts.why: CTEs turn nested, hard-to-read subqueries into a series of named steps a reader can follow from top to bottom.
concepts.body:
A **common table expression** (CTE) names a subquery up front with `WITH`, so the main query can use it like a table:

```sql
WITH spend AS (
    SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS spent
    FROM orders WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT c.name, s.spent
FROM spend s JOIN customers c ON c.id = s.customer_id;
```

Several CTEs can be chained, separated by commas, and each may refer to the ones before it. A query becomes a readable series of steps: compute per-customer spend, then rank it, then keep the top rows. A CTE can also be referenced more than once in the main query, which a derived table cannot.

Performance used to be the catch. Before PostgreSQL 12, every CTE was an **optimisation fence**: it was computed in full and stored first, and the query planner could not push the outer query's filters into it. Since version 12, a CTE that only reads data and is used once is **inlined**: merged into the main query like a subquery, and optimised together with it. You can choose explicitly. `WITH x AS MATERIALIZED (...)` forces it to be computed once and stored (useful when it is expensive and used several times), and `AS NOT MATERIALIZED` forces inlining. Other databases make their own choices; SQL Server always inlines, for example.

PostgreSQL also allows **data-modifying CTEs**: `INSERT`, `UPDATE` or `DELETE ... RETURNING` inside `WITH`. That moves rows between tables in a single statement, which either fully succeeds or changes nothing:

```sql
WITH moved AS (
    DELETE FROM orders WHERE status = 'cancelled' RETURNING *
)
INSERT INTO orders_archive SELECT * FROM moved;
```

All parts of such a statement see the data as it was when the statement started, so one CTE cannot see rows another CTE in the same statement just changed; pass them on through `RETURNING` instead.
concepts.code:
WITH spend AS (
    SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS spent
    FROM orders
    WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
    GROUP BY customer_id
),
average AS (
    SELECT AVG(spent) AS avg_spent FROM spend
)
SELECT c.name, s.spent
FROM spend s
JOIN customers c ON c.id = s.customer_id
CROSS JOIN average a
WHERE s.spent > a.avg_spent;          -- avg of 257.50 and 247.99 = 252.745
--  name | spent
--  Ana  | 257.50

-- Force a single evaluation of an expensive CTE used twice
WITH heavy AS MATERIALIZED (
    SELECT product_id, SUM(quantity) AS sold FROM order_items GROUP BY product_id
)
SELECT (SELECT MAX(sold) FROM heavy) AS best, (SELECT MIN(sold) FROM heavy) AS worst;
--  best | worst
--     3 |     1
takeaways: WITH names intermediate results so a query reads top to bottom
Since PostgreSQL 12, single-use CTEs are merged into the main query; MATERIALIZED / NOT MATERIALIZED force either choice
Data-modifying CTEs with RETURNING move data in one all-or-nothing statement
pitfalls: Assuming a CTE is always computed once and stored; in modern PostgreSQL it may be merged into the main query and planned with it.

quiz.q: In PostgreSQL 12+, what happens to a side-effect-free CTE referenced once in the main query?
options: It is always materialised to a temporary table
It is executed after the main query
It is inlined into the main query and optimised with it
quiz.explain: Single-reference, non-recursive, side-effect-free CTEs are inlined unless you write MATERIALIZED.

quiz.q: What is a reason to use a CTE instead of a derived table in FROM?
options: A CTE can be referenced several times and reads in order
Derived tables cannot contain GROUP BY
quiz.explain: A named CTE can be reused within the query and makes multi-step logic readable.

concepts.name: Recursive CTEs and hierarchies
concepts.summary: Walk trees and graphs such as category hierarchies with WITH RECURSIVE.
concepts.why: Hierarchies (categories, org charts, threaded comments) cannot be traversed to arbitrary depth with plain joins.
concepts.body:
Stored hierarchies usually look like `categories(id, parent_id, name)`: each row points at its parent. A join finds one level; finding all descendants, at any depth, needs **recursion**: a step that is applied again to its own output until nothing new comes out.

A **recursive CTE** has two parts joined by `UNION ALL`, which stacks the rows of both:

1. The **anchor** (non-recursive term) produces the starting rows.
2. The **recursive term** refers to the CTE itself and produces the next level from the rows of the previous step.

PostgreSQL evaluates the anchor, then repeatedly runs the recursive term against only the rows produced in the previous round (each round is an **iteration**), until a round produces nothing. The result is everything accumulated.

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
    SELECT id, name, 1 AS depth FROM categories WHERE id = 2       -- anchor
    UNION ALL
    SELECT c.id, c.name, t.depth + 1
    FROM categories c JOIN tree t ON c.parent_id = t.id             -- step
)
SELECT * FROM tree;
```

Carrying extra columns along is the main trick: a `depth` counter, or a `path` built by appending to a list value (a PostgreSQL **array**) or a string, which also sorts the output in tree order.

The danger is **cycles**. If the data ever goes round in a circle (A's parent is B, B's parent is A), `UNION ALL` recursion never ends. Defences: use `UNION` instead (stops when no new distinct rows appear, but only works if rows repeat exactly), keep a path array and stop when the id is already in it, or use PostgreSQL 14's standard `CYCLE id SET is_cycle USING path` clause. A depth limit in the recursive term (`WHERE t.depth < 20`) is a cheap safety net.

Recursive CTEs also generate sequences. Dialects: the standard and PostgreSQL, MySQL 8 and SQLite need the `RECURSIVE` keyword; SQL Server and Oracle omit it, and older Oracle code uses `CONNECT BY`.
concepts.code:
-- categories: 1 All (parent NULL), 2 Hardware (1), 3 Input devices (2),
--             4 Displays (2), 5 Digital (1), 6 Keyboards (3)
WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
    SELECT id, name, 1 AS depth, ARRAY[name] AS path
    FROM categories
    WHERE id = 2                                   -- start at Hardware
    UNION ALL
    SELECT c.id, c.name, t.depth + 1, t.path || c.name
    FROM categories c
    JOIN tree t ON c.parent_id = t.id
    WHERE t.depth < 20                             -- safety net
)
SELECT repeat('  ', depth - 1) || name AS category, depth
FROM tree
ORDER BY path;
--  category          | depth
--  Hardware          |     1
--    Displays        |     2
--    Input devices   |     2
--      Keyboards     |     3
takeaways: A recursive CTE is an anchor, UNION ALL, and a step that uses the CTE itself
Each iteration sees only the previous iteration's new rows
Carry depth and path columns to label and sort the tree
Guard against cycles: CYCLE clause, path checks or a depth limit
pitfalls: Recursing over data with a cycle using UNION ALL and no guard, producing a query that never finishes.

quiz.q: In WITH RECURSIVE, which rows does the recursive term see on each iteration?
options: Only the rows produced by the previous iteration
quiz.explain: PostgreSQL feeds the recursive term the working table of the last iteration's output, which is why recursion ends when a step adds nothing.

quiz.q: Why sort a tree query by an accumulated path array?
options: It places each node directly under its ancestors, giving tree order
ORDER BY depth is not allowed in recursive CTEs
quiz.explain: Comparing paths element by element groups descendants beneath their parent.

concepts.name: Window functions
concepts.summary: Compute rankings, running totals and row-to-row comparisons with OVER, without collapsing rows.
concepts.why: Top-N per group, period-over-period change and cumulative sums are window-function problems.
concepts.body:
An aggregate with `GROUP BY` collapses each group to one row. A **window function** computes over a set of related rows but keeps every row, adding the result as a column. The `OVER` clause defines the window:

```sql
SUM(total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_at)
```

- `PARTITION BY` splits rows into independent groups, called partitions (like `GROUP BY`, without collapsing). Omit it to use the whole result.
- `ORDER BY` orders rows within each partition. For aggregates like `SUM` it also makes the result **cumulative**: a running total.

Key functions:

- `row_number()` numbers rows 1, 2, 3; `rank()` gives ties the same number and leaves gaps (1, 1, 3); `dense_rank()` leaves none (1, 1, 2).
- `lag(x)` and `lead(x)` read a value from the previous or next row, for differences between consecutive rows.
- `first_value`, `last_value`, `ntile(n)`, and any ordinary aggregate.

The **window frame** decides which rows of the partition an aggregate sees. With `ORDER BY`, the default is `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`, which includes rows tied with the current one (its peers): two orders at the same date and time get the same running total. Say `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` if you want strictly row-by-row, or `ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` for a 7-row moving average. The default frame is also why `last_value` surprises people: it stops at the current row.

Window functions run after `WHERE`, `GROUP BY` and `HAVING`, so you cannot filter on them in `WHERE`. Wrap the query in a CTE or subquery and filter outside; that is the standard way to get the top N rows per group. Snowflake, BigQuery and DuckDB offer a `QUALIFY` clause for this; PostgreSQL does not.
concepts.code:
SELECT customer_id, id, total,
       SUM(total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_at) AS running,
       lag(total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_at) AS prev,
       rank()     OVER (ORDER BY total DESC)                           AS overall_rank
FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id, ordered_at;
--  customer_id | id  | total  | running | prev  | overall_rank
--            1 | 101 |  68.50 |   68.50 |  NULL |            3
--            1 | 102 | 189.00 |  257.50 | 68.50 |            2
--            2 | 103 |   9.99 |    9.99 |  NULL |            5
--            2 | 105 | 238.00 |  247.99 |  9.99 |            1
--            3 | 104 |  49.00 |   49.00 |  NULL |            4

-- Top order per customer: filter outside the window query
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT customer_id, id, total,
           row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY total DESC) AS rn
    FROM orders
)
SELECT customer_id, id, total FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;
--  1 | 102 | 189.00
--  2 | 105 | 238.00
--  3 | 104 |  49.00
takeaways: Window functions add a computed column without collapsing rows
PARTITION BY groups, ORDER BY orders and makes aggregates cumulative
Default frame with ORDER BY includes peers; use ROWS for strict row frames
Filter on window results in an outer query (no QUALIFY in PostgreSQL)
pitfalls: Using last_value() with the default frame and getting the current row's value.

quiz.q: Totals 50, 50, 40 ranked by total DESC. What do rank() and dense_rank() give?
quiz.explain: rank() leaves a gap after ties; dense_rank() does not.

quiz.q: Why does WHERE row_number() OVER (...) = 1 fail?
options: Window functions only work in ORDER BY
Window functions are evaluated after WHERE, so they cannot appear in it
quiz.explain: Compute the window in a subquery or CTE and filter in the outer query.

concepts.name: UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT
concepts.summary: Combine the results of whole queries by stacking, intersecting or subtracting their rows.
concepts.why: Merging similar data from several sources, or finding what is in one set but not another, is a set operation.
concepts.body:
Joins combine tables side by side; **set operations** combine query results vertically. Each takes two queries with the same number of columns, in compatible types, and treats their results as sets of rows:

- `UNION` returns rows that appear in either query, **removing duplicates**.
- `UNION ALL` returns all rows from both, keeping duplicates.
- `INTERSECT` returns rows present in both.
- `EXCEPT` returns rows in the first query but not the second. Oracle traditionally calls it `MINUS`; MySQL added `INTERSECT` and `EXCEPT` only in 8.0.31.

Prefer `UNION ALL` whenever duplicates are impossible or wanted. Plain `UNION` must compare all the rows to remove duplicates, which is wasted work on large results.

Columns are matched by **position**, not name, and the output takes its column names from the first query. Lining up the wrong columns gives silently wrong results as long as the types are compatible, so write the select lists so they visibly line up.

`ORDER BY` and `LIMIT` apply to the combined result and go at the very end. To sort or limit one branch, wrap it in parentheses.

Unlike `=`, set operations treat two NULLs as duplicates of each other, the same way `DISTINCT` does. That makes `EXCEPT` a convenient NULL-safe way to compare two tables row by row: `(SELECT * FROM a EXCEPT SELECT * FROM b)` lists rows of `a` missing from `b`.

Precedence: `INTERSECT` binds tighter than `UNION` and `EXCEPT`. Use parentheses when you mix them.
concepts.code:
-- Customers who ordered in February / March
-- Feb: customers 1, 2      Mar: customers 3, 2

SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE ordered_at >= '2026-02-01' AND ordered_at < '2026-03-01'
INTERSECT
SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE ordered_at >= '2026-03-01' AND ordered_at < '2026-04-01';
--  2                         (ordered in both months)

SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE ordered_at >= '2026-02-01' AND ordered_at < '2026-03-01'
EXCEPT
SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE ordered_at >= '2026-03-01' AND ordered_at < '2026-04-01';
--  1                         (February but not March)

-- Stack two sources into one list; names come from the first query
SELECT name, 'customer' AS kind FROM customers
UNION ALL
SELECT name, 'product' FROM products
ORDER BY kind, name;          -- applies to the whole result
takeaways: UNION removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps them and is cheaper
INTERSECT = in both; EXCEPT = in the first but not the second
Columns match by position; names come from the first query
Set operations treat NULLs as equal, unlike =
pitfalls: Using UNION where UNION ALL is correct, paying for a needless de-duplication sort.

quiz.q: Query A returns customer ids 1, 2 and query B returns 2, 3. How many rows does A UNION ALL B return?
quiz.explain: UNION ALL keeps every row from both sides, including the duplicate 2.

quiz.q: SELECT name, city ... UNION SELECT city, name ... runs without error. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, UNION matches columns by name
The second query's names are used for the output
Columns are matched by position, so names and cities are mixed in the same column
quiz.explain: Set operations line up columns by their position in the select list.

concepts.name: Upserts: ON CONFLICT and MERGE
concepts.summary: Insert a row, or update it if it already exists, in one safe statement with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT or MERGE.
concepts.why: Syncing data, counters and actions that may be sent twice all need 'insert or update' that can't go wrong when two happen at once.
concepts.body:
"Insert unless it exists, otherwise update" looks like a `SELECT` followed by an `INSERT` or `UPDATE`. When two requests arrive at the same moment, that is a **race condition**: both see no row, both insert, and one fails or duplicates data. Do it in one **atomic** statement instead, one that happens completely or not at all, with nothing able to slip in between.

Insert-or-update is called an **upsert**. PostgreSQL's version is `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT`:

```sql
INSERT INTO customers (email, name) VALUES ('ana@example.com', 'Ana K.')
ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name;
```

- The conflict target `(email)` must match a unique index or constraint; that index is what detects the conflict.
- `EXCLUDED` refers to the row you tried to insert; the plain table name refers to the existing row. That allows increments: `SET qty = daily_sales.qty + EXCLUDED.qty`.
- `DO UPDATE ... WHERE` updates only when a condition holds, for example only if the incoming data is newer.
- `DO NOTHING` silently skips rows that already exist, which makes inserts **idempotent**: running the same insert twice has the same effect as running it once.

One multi-row `INSERT` cannot touch the same row twice: if two input rows share an email, PostgreSQL raises "ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time". De-duplicate the input first.

`MERGE` (SQL standard; PostgreSQL 15+, SQL Server, Oracle) is more general: it joins a source to a target and runs different actions `WHEN MATCHED` and `WHEN NOT MATCHED`, including deletes. It is ideal for bringing a table up to date in bulk from a table where new data was loaded first. In PostgreSQL, however, `MERGE` is not protected against inserts happening at the same time the way `ON CONFLICT` is: two `MERGE`s running at once can both decide to insert, and one then fails with a unique violation. When many single-row upserts run at once, prefer `ON CONFLICT`.

MySQL's equivalent is `INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`; SQLite understands PostgreSQL's `ON CONFLICT` form.
concepts.code:
CREATE TABLE daily_sales (
    product_id bigint REFERENCES products (id),
    day        date,
    qty        integer NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (product_id, day)
);

-- Atomic counter: insert the first sale, increment afterwards
INSERT INTO daily_sales (product_id, day, qty) VALUES (2, '2026-03-15', 1)
ON CONFLICT (product_id, day)
DO UPDATE SET qty = daily_sales.qty + EXCLUDED.qty
RETURNING qty;          -- 1 the first time, 2 the second time, ...

-- Idempotent insert
INSERT INTO customers (name, email) VALUES ('Ana', 'ana@example.com')
ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING;     -- INSERT 0 0

-- Batch sync from a staging table (PostgreSQL 15+)
MERGE INTO products p
USING staged_products s ON s.sku = p.sku
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET price = s.price
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (sku, name, price) VALUES (s.sku, s.name, s.price);
takeaways: Never SELECT-then-INSERT for upserts; two requests at once can both insert
ON CONFLICT needs a unique index on the conflict target; EXCLUDED is the proposed row
DO NOTHING makes inserts idempotent
MERGE suits bulk updates from another table; ON CONFLICT is safer when many upserts run at once in PostgreSQL
pitfalls: Including the same key twice in one multi-row upsert, which fails with 'cannot affect row a second time'.

quiz.q: In ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name, what is EXCLUDED?
options: The existing row in the table
The row that was proposed for insertion
A table of rows that failed constraints
quiz.explain: EXCLUDED holds the values you tried to insert; the table name refers to the existing row.

quiz.q: Why is 'SELECT the row; if missing INSERT, else UPDATE' unsafe in application code?
options: Two concurrent requests can both see no row and both try to insert
SELECT cannot see uncommitted rows of the same session
It is safe if wrapped in any transaction
quiz.explain: Between the check and the write another transaction can act; a single atomic upsert closes that window.

concepts.name: Normalization and schema design
concepts.summary: Design tables so each fact is stored once, and know when deliberate denormalization is worth it.
concepts.why: A well-normalised schema prevents contradictory data; a badly designed one causes mistakes no query can fix.
concepts.body:
**Normalization** is the discipline of storing each fact in exactly one place. Duplicated facts drift apart: if a customer's city is stored on every order, changing it means updating many rows, and missing one leaves the data contradicting itself (an **update anomaly**).

The normal forms are a checklist for spotting that duplication:

- **First normal form (1NF)**: each column holds a single value. No comma-separated lists like `product_ids = '1,3,4'`; they cannot be joined, indexed or constrained. Use a row per value in a child table.
- **Second normal form (2NF)**: in a table with a composite key, every non-key column depends on the whole key. In `order_items (order_id, product_id, ...)`, a `product_name` column depends only on `product_id`, so it belongs in `products`.
- **Third normal form (3NF)**: non-key columns depend on the key and nothing else. If `customers` stored both `city` and `country`, and country is determined by city, that fact belongs in a `cities` table.

The short version: every non-key column should describe "the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key".

Many-to-many relationships, where each product can have many tags and each tag many products, need a **junction table** `product_tags (product_id, tag_id)` with a composite primary key and two foreign keys.

Not every repeated value is a violation. `order_items.unit_price` looks like a copy of `products.price`, but it records a historical fact: the price when the order was placed. If prices change, past orders must not. Ask whether the value should change when the source changes.

**Denormalization**, storing derived or duplicated data on purpose, is a legitimate optimisation for data that is read far more often than it changes, such as a stored `orders.total` or a table built for reports. Do it deliberately and keep one source of truth. Keep the copy up to date with transactions, with **triggers** (code the database runs automatically when rows change), or with materialized views (stored query results).
concepts.code:
-- Not normalised: lists in a column, product facts repeated per order
-- orders_bad(id, customer_name, customer_city, product_ids text, product_names text)
--   101 | Ana | Yerevan | '1,2' | 'Keyboard,Mouse'

-- Normalised: each fact in one place, linked by keys
CREATE TABLE tags (
    id   bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    name text NOT NULL UNIQUE
);

CREATE TABLE product_tags (                    -- many-to-many junction
    product_id bigint REFERENCES products (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    tag_id     bigint REFERENCES tags (id)     ON DELETE CASCADE,
    PRIMARY KEY (product_id, tag_id)
);
CREATE INDEX ON product_tags (tag_id);         -- for tag -> products lookups

-- Products carrying a tag: a join, not string parsing
SELECT p.name
FROM products p
JOIN product_tags pt ON pt.product_id = p.id
JOIN tags t          ON t.id = pt.tag_id
WHERE t.name = 'wireless';
takeaways: Store each fact once; duplicated facts drift apart
1NF: no lists in columns; 2NF/3NF: columns depend on the whole key and nothing else
Many-to-many relationships need a junction table
Values recorded at a moment in history (like unit_price) are not duplication; denormalize only deliberately
pitfalls: Storing comma-separated ids in a text column instead of a child table.

quiz.q: order_items (order_id, product_id, quantity, product_name) has key (order_id, product_id). Which normal form does product_name violate?
quiz.explain: product_name depends on only part of the composite key (product_id): a partial dependency, which 2NF forbids.

quiz.q: Why is order_items.unit_price not a harmful duplicate of products.price?
options: It records the price at the time of sale, a different fact from today's price
Duplicated numeric columns are always acceptable
quiz.explain: The two values are meant to diverge when the catalogue price changes.

concepts.name: Reading query plans with EXPLAIN
concepts.summary: Use EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE to see how PostgreSQL executes a query and where the time goes.
concepts.why: Guessing at slow queries wastes days; the plan tells you what is actually happening.
concepts.body:
`EXPLAIN` shows the **query plan** the query planner chose, its step-by-step strategy: a tree of nodes, each producing rows for its parent. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` actually runs the query and adds real timings and row counts. Because it executes the statement, wrap data-modifying queries in `BEGIN; EXPLAIN ANALYZE ...; ROLLBACK;`.

Each node line looks like:

```
Index Scan using orders_customer_id_idx on orders
  (cost=0.43..8.45 rows=3 width=48) (actual time=0.020..0.024 rows=2 loops=1)
```

- `cost=startup..total` is in arbitrary planner units (roughly, how many small fixed-size blocks of storage, called pages, it expects to read in order). Use it to compare plans, not as milliseconds.
- `rows` is the estimate; `actual ... rows` is reality. `actual time` is in milliseconds **per run of that step**, and `loops` says how many times it ran: multiply them.
- Child nodes are indented below their parent; execution data flows upward.

Common nodes: `Seq Scan` (read the whole table), `Index Scan`, `Index Only Scan` (answered from the index alone), `Bitmap Heap Scan` (collect many matches from an index, then read pages in order), `Nested Loop`, `Hash Join`, `Merge Join`, `Sort`, `HashAggregate`.

How to read a slow plan:

1. Find the nodes where actual time jumps.
2. Compare estimated and actual rows. An estimate off by 100x usually means the planner chose a bad way or order to join; the cause is often out-of-date statistics (the planner's summary of what each column contains, covered in the planner lesson).
3. Look for `Seq Scan` on large tables behind a filter that keeps few rows (a missing index), `Rows Removed by Filter` in the millions, or a `Sort` spilling to disk (`Sort Method: external merge`).

Add `BUFFERS` (`EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`) to see how many pages came straight from memory and how many had to be read from disk. Tools like explain.dalibo.com visualise large plans.
concepts.code:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT c.name, SUM(o.total)
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.ordered_at >= '2026-03-01'
GROUP BY c.name;
-- HashAggregate  (cost=245.1..247.6 rows=200 width=64)
--                (actual time=4.91..4.95 rows=180 loops=1)
--   Group Key: c.name
--   ->  Hash Join  (cost=38.5..236.3 rows=1760 width=38)
--                  (actual time=0.61..4.12 rows=1802 loops=1)
--         Hash Cond: (o.customer_id = c.id)
--         ->  Seq Scan on orders o  (cost=0.0..193.0 rows=1760 width=14)
--                                   (actual time=0.01..3.02 rows=1802 loops=1)
--               Filter: (ordered_at >= '2026-03-01 00:00:00+00')
--               Rows Removed by Filter: 8198
--         ->  Hash  (actual time=0.55..0.55 rows=1000 loops=1)
--               ->  Seq Scan on customers c  (...)
-- Planning Time: 0.31 ms
-- Execution Time: 5.10 ms

-- Safely analyse a write
BEGIN;
EXPLAIN ANALYZE UPDATE orders SET status = 'shipped' WHERE id = 102;
ROLLBACK;
takeaways: EXPLAIN shows the chosen plan; EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs it and reports reality
Costs are relative units; actual time is ms per run of a step
Big gaps between estimated and actual rows point to statistics problems
EXPLAIN ANALYZE really runs writes; wrap them in BEGIN ... ROLLBACK
pitfalls: Running EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a DELETE on the live database and actually deleting the rows.

quiz.q: A node shows actual time=0.050..0.050 rows=1 loops=2000. Roughly how long did it take in total?
quiz.explain: Actual time is per loop, so 0.05 ms x 2000 loops is about 100 ms.

quiz.q: Estimated rows=5 but actual rows=48000 on a scan feeding a Nested Loop. What is the most likely root issue?
options: Misestimated row count, often from stale or insufficient statistics, led to a poor join choice
The query has no ORDER BY
quiz.explain: A nested loop is chosen for few outer rows; a 10,000x misestimate makes that choice disastrous.

concepts.name: Advanced indexing
concepts.summary: Use expression, partial and covering indexes, and pick another index type when a plain B-tree is not enough.
concepts.why: The right specialised index can turn a full scan into a millisecond lookup at a fraction of the size.
concepts.body:
Beyond the plain B-tree, PostgreSQL offers several ways to make an index fit a query exactly.

An **expression index** indexes a computed value. A query on `lower(email)` cannot use an index on `email`, but it can use one on `lower(email)`. The query must use the same expression.

A **partial index** covers only the rows matching a condition: `CREATE INDEX ON orders (ordered_at) WHERE status = 'pending'`. If pending orders are 1% of the table, the index is 1% of the size, and queries that include `status = 'pending'` can use it. A unique partial index enforces rules like "at most one active subscription per customer".

A **covering index** stores extra columns with `INCLUDE`: `CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id) INCLUDE (total)`. A query needing only those columns can be answered by an **index-only scan**, without visiting the table. That works only for parts of the table with no recent changes waiting to be cleaned up, so it depends on PostgreSQL's background cleanup keeping up (a later lesson on row versions explains why).

Other index types, each for a different kind of data:

- **GIN**: for values holding many items each. Use it for JSON documents (structured text data, covered next), PostgreSQL **arrays** (list values stored in one column), searching words inside text, and, with the `pg_trgm` add-on, `LIKE '%term%'` searches.
- **GiST**: for shapes, locations and ranges of values, and 'what is nearest?' searches (the PostGIS maps add-on uses it). It also enforces rules such as 'no overlapping bookings'.
- **BRIN**: stores only min/max per block range. Tiny, and very effective on huge tables whose values follow the order rows were stored in, such as `created_at` on a table where rows are only ever added. Useless when values are scattered.
- **Hash** indexes: exact-equality lookups only; rarely better than a B-tree.

Every index adds write cost. Check `pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan` periodically and drop indexes that are never used.
takeaways: Expression indexes serve queries that use the same expression
Partial indexes are small and can enforce uniqueness among some rows only
INCLUDE columns enable index-only scans
GIN for JSON, arrays and word search; GiST for ranges and shapes; BRIN for huge ordered tables
pitfalls: Creating an expression index on lower(email) but querying WHERE email ILIKE ..., which cannot use it.

quiz.q: Which index best serves WHERE status = 'pending' ORDER BY ordered_at when 1% of orders are pending?
options: CREATE INDEX ON orders (ordered_at) WHERE status = 'pending'
CREATE INDEX ON orders USING hash (status)
CREATE INDEX ON orders USING brin (status)
quiz.explain: The partial index contains only pending rows, already sorted by ordered_at.

quiz.q: When is a BRIN index a good choice?
options: A very large table where the column's values correlate with physical row order
quiz.explain: BRIN stores ranges per block, so it only prunes well when nearby rows have nearby values.

concepts.name: JSON columns with jsonb
concepts.summary: Store, query and index semi-structured data in PostgreSQL jsonb columns, and know when not to.
concepts.why: Details that vary from row to row, and data received from other systems, fit poorly in fixed columns; jsonb handles them inside SQL.
concepts.body:
**JSON** is a common text format for structured data, such as `{"wireless": true, "dpi": 1600}`: names (keys) paired with values, which can nest. PostgreSQL has two column types for it. `json` stores the text exactly as given. **jsonb** converts it once, on the way in, into a ready-to-search internal form; it drops repeated keys and extra spaces, and supports indexes and many operators. Use `jsonb` unless you must keep the exact input text.

Operators to know:

- `attrs -> 'dpi'` returns a `jsonb` value; `attrs ->> 'dpi'` returns `text`. Cast for comparisons: `(attrs ->> 'dpi')::int > 1000`.
- `attrs #>> '{dims,width}'` follows a path.
- `attrs @> '{"wireless": true}'` tests **containment**: does the left document contain this structure?
- `attrs ? 'dpi'` tests whether a top-level key exists.
- `attrs || '{"color": "black"}'` merges; `attrs - 'dpi'` removes a key; `jsonb_set` replaces a nested value.

Functions such as `jsonb_array_elements` and `jsonb_each` expand JSON into rows, and `jsonb_build_object` and `jsonb_agg` build JSON from rows, handy when an app wants its data as JSON. PostgreSQL also implements the SQL/JSON standard: `jsonb_path_query` with JSONPath, and in version 17, `JSON_TABLE` to turn documents into relational rows.

Indexing: a GIN index on the column (`USING gin (attrs)`) speeds up `@>`, `?` and related operators. Its `jsonb_path_ops` variant is smaller and faster but supports only containment and path searches. For one key you filter on often, a B-tree expression index on `(attrs ->> 'brand')` is better.

Use `jsonb` for data that genuinely varies: product details that differ by category, messages received from other services, user settings. Don't use it to avoid designing a schema. Values every row has, values you join on or put rules on, and anything a foreign key points at belong in real columns, where types, rules and the planner's statistics all work properly.

MySQL has a `JSON` type with similar `->` / `->>` operators; SQL Server stores JSON in text columns with `JSON_VALUE` functions.
takeaways: Prefer jsonb over json
-> returns jsonb, ->> returns text; @> tests containment
GIN indexes accelerate containment; expression indexes serve single keys
Keep core values, and values you join on or put rules on, in real columns
pitfalls: Comparing attrs -> 'dpi' (a jsonb value) with a plain number or text instead of converting attrs ->> 'dpi'.

quiz.q: What type does attrs ->> 'dpi' return?
quiz.explain: ->> extracts the value as text; -> keeps it as jsonb.

quiz.q: Which index supports WHERE attrs @> '{"wireless": true}' on a large table?
quiz.explain: GIN indexes the keys and values inside each document, which is what containment needs.

concepts.name: MVCC, row versions and VACUUM
concepts.summary: How PostgreSQL keeps multiple row versions so readers never block writers, and why VACUUM must clean them up.
concepts.why: MVCC explains table bloat, slow counts, vacuum load and the cost of long-running transactions.
concepts.body:
PostgreSQL keeps transactions from seeing each other's unfinished work with **multi-version concurrency control** (MVCC). It never overwrites a row in place. An `UPDATE` writes a complete new **row version** and marks the old one as expired; a `DELETE` only marks it. Each version carries hidden columns: `xmin`, the id of the transaction that created it, and `xmax`, the one that deleted or replaced it.

Every statement (or, under the stricter settings in the next lesson, every transaction) runs against a **snapshot**: the set of transactions that had committed at the moment it was taken. A row version is visible if its creator had committed by then and its deleter had not. Consequences:

- Readers never block writers, and writers never block readers. A long report reads consistent data while updates continue.
- Two writers on the **same row** still conflict; the second waits for the first to finish.
- `SELECT count(*)` must check visibility, so it cannot simply read a stored counter.

Expired row versions that no snapshot can see any more are **dead tuples**. **VACUUM** removes them and makes their space reusable (it rarely shrinks the file; `VACUUM FULL` rewrites the table but locks everyone out meanwhile). It also records which parts of the table have no pending changes, which lets some queries be answered from an index alone.

VACUUM also marks old rows as safely old ('freezing'), to prevent **transaction ID wraparound**: transaction ids come from a counter that eventually runs out and starts again, and without freezing the database would have to stop accepting writes. **Autovacuum** does all this in the background, started by the number of changed rows.

The classic way to break it is a transaction left open for hours, such as an abandoned 'idle in transaction' connection, or a forgotten replication slot (see the replication lesson). As long as an old snapshot might need old versions, VACUUM can't remove them, and frequently updated tables fill with wasted space, called **bloat**. Watch `n_dead_tup` and `pg_stat_activity.xact_start`.

**HOT** updates soften the write cost: if no indexed column changes and the same small storage block (page) has room, the new version goes on that page and the indexes need no new entries.
takeaways: UPDATE writes a new row version; DELETE only marks the old one expired
Snapshots decide visibility: readers and writers do not block each other
VACUUM removes dead tuples, helps index-only reads and prevents transaction ID wraparound
Long-open transactions stop cleanup and cause bloat
pitfalls: Disabling autovacuum on a busy table to 'save resources', leading to bloat and eventually wraparound emergencies.

quiz.q: A report runs a 30-minute SELECT while other sessions update the same table. What happens in PostgreSQL?
options: The updates wait until the report finishes
The report sees each update as soon as it commits, mid-scan
The report fails with a serialization error
The report sees a consistent snapshot while updates proceed
quiz.explain: MVCC gives the reader its own snapshot; writers create new versions without blocking it.

quiz.q: Why can a session idle in transaction for hours cause table bloat?
options: It holds an exclusive table lock
VACUUM cannot remove row versions that its old snapshot might still need
quiz.explain: Dead tuples are only removable once no running transaction could still see them.

concepts.name: Isolation levels and anomalies
concepts.summary: What READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE guarantee in PostgreSQL, and which anomalies each allows.
concepts.why: Mistakes that only appear when transactions run at the same time pass every test and then corrupt live data.
concepts.body:
An **isolation level** is a setting that decides how much transactions running at the same time see of each other's changes. The SQL standard defines the levels by the anomalies (wrong results) they forbid:

- **dirty reads**: seeing data another transaction hasn't committed yet,
- **non-repeatable reads**: a row changes between two reads in the same transaction,
- **phantom reads**: new rows appear when a query is repeated,
- **serialization anomalies**: a result that would be impossible if the transactions had run one at a time.

PostgreSQL implements three distinct levels.

**Read Committed** (the default in PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server) takes a new snapshot for each statement. Dirty reads never happen, but two statements in one transaction can see different data. Its classic mistake is the **lost update**, done in app code: two connections read `stock = 5`, both compute 4, both write 4. Fix it by doing the arithmetic in SQL (`SET stock = stock - 1`), which re-reads the latest committed row, or by locking the row with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`.

**Repeatable Read** takes one snapshot at the first statement, so the whole transaction sees a frozen view. In PostgreSQL this is snapshot isolation and also prevents phantoms. If you try to update a row someone else changed and committed after your snapshot, you get `ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update` (SQLSTATE `40001`). What it still allows is **write skew**, where two transactions each check a rule and then change different rows: two doctors each check "is someone else on call?", both see yes, both go off call. Each transaction was valid alone; together they broke the rule.

**Serializable** uses serializable snapshot isolation (SSI): it tracks which transactions read data that others changed, and cancels one transaction, again with `40001`, when the outcome could not have arisen serially. It prevents write skew with no explicit locks.

At Repeatable Read and Serializable, **your app must run again** any transaction that fails with `40001`. That is part of the contract, not an exceptional failure.

Dialects: `READ UNCOMMITTED` behaves as Read Committed in PostgreSQL. MySQL InnoDB defaults to Repeatable Read, with different, lock-based semantics.
takeaways: Read Committed: new snapshot per statement; watch for lost updates
Repeatable Read: one snapshot per transaction; still allows write skew
Serializable (SSI) prevents all anomalies by aborting conflicting transactions
At Repeatable Read and Serializable, rerun transactions that fail with error 40001
pitfalls: Raising the isolation level without adding code that reruns failed transactions, turning wrong results into unhandled errors.

quiz.q: Under PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ, transaction A updates a row that B modified and committed after A's snapshot. What happens?
options: A fails with a serialization error (40001) and should be retried
A sees B's change and proceeds
quiz.explain: Snapshot isolation refuses to update a row version newer than the transaction's snapshot.

quiz.q: Which anomaly does PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ still permit?
quiz.explain: Two transactions reading overlapping data and writing disjoint rows can break an invariant; only SERIALIZABLE detects this.

concepts.name: Locks, SKIP LOCKED and deadlocks
concepts.summary: Row and table locks in PostgreSQL, locking rows yourself with FOR UPDATE, job queues, and how deadlocks arise.
concepts.why: Waiting for locks is behind most mysterious freezes on live systems, from job queues to migrations that stall a whole site.
concepts.body:
MVCC means readers and writers don't wait for each other, but two writers still do. `UPDATE`, `DELETE` and `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` take **row-level locks** held until the transaction ends. A second transaction trying to modify the same row waits.

Explicit row locks come in four strengths: `FOR UPDATE` (exclusive), `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` (taken by ordinary updates that do not change keys), `FOR SHARE` and `FOR KEY SHARE` (taken when foreign keys are checked). Two modifiers change waiting behaviour:

- `NOWAIT` errors immediately instead of waiting.
- `SKIP LOCKED` silently skips locked rows. That turns a table into a safe **job queue**, a list of tasks waiting to be done: many copies of a background program run `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1` and never grab the same job.

**Table-level locks** are taken by every statement. Most are compatible with each other, but many `ALTER TABLE` forms, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE` and `VACUUM FULL` need `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`, which conflicts with everything, including plain `SELECT`. Lock requests wait in line, in order: a migration waiting behind one long transaction blocks every query that arrives after it. Always set `lock_timeout` in migrations so they give up quickly and can be run again, instead of freezing the app.

A **deadlock** occurs when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs. Neither can ever continue, so PostgreSQL checks for such circles after `deadlock_timeout` (1 second by default) and cancels one transaction with `ERROR: deadlock detected` (error code `40P01`). Prevent them by locking rows in a **consistent order** (for example by ascending id) and keeping transactions short; handle the occasional one by running the transaction again.

For locks on things that are not rows, such as 'only one copy of the nightly job runs', use **advisory locks**, locks on a number you choose: `pg_try_advisory_lock(42)`.

Diagnose with `pg_locks` and `pg_blocking_pids(pid)`.
takeaways: Row locks from writes and FOR UPDATE last until commit or rollback
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED builds safe concurrent job queues
ACCESS EXCLUSIVE locks queue and block even reads; use lock_timeout for DDL
Prevent deadlocks with a consistent lock order; rerun the transaction on error 40P01
pitfalls: Running ALTER TABLE on a hot table without lock_timeout, so it queues behind a long query and blocks all traffic.

quiz.q: Several workers poll a jobs table. Which clause lets each take a different job without waiting?
quiz.explain: SKIP LOCKED passes over rows other transactions hold, so each worker locks the next free job.

quiz.q: A long SELECT is running. An ALTER TABLE on the same table starts waiting. What happens to new SELECTs?
options: They run normally, since SELECTs never block
They read the table's previous version
They queue behind the waiting ALTER TABLE's ACCESS EXCLUSIVE request
quiz.explain: Lock requests queue in order; a pending ACCESS EXCLUSIVE request conflicts with later reads, which then wait too.

concepts.name: The query planner and statistics
concepts.summary: How PostgreSQL's planner estimates row counts from statistics, and how it decides how, and in what order, to combine tables.
concepts.why: When a plan goes wrong, the cause is almost always a bad estimate; fixing it requires knowing where estimates come from.
concepts.body:
PostgreSQL's planner is **cost-based**: it enumerates candidate plans, estimates the cost of each, and picks the cheapest. Costs combine page reads (`seq_page_cost` = 1, `random_page_cost` = 4 by default; values near 1.1 suit SSDs) with the processing cost of each row. Everything hinges on **row-count estimates**.

Estimates come from statistics: summaries of each column's contents gathered by `ANALYZE` (which PostgreSQL's background cleanup also runs automatically). It samples rows (300 times `default_statistics_target`, so 30,000 at the default of 100) and stores, per column, in `pg_stats`: the fraction of NULLs, the number of distinct values, the **most common values** with their frequencies, a **histogram** of the rest (how many values fall into each range), and how closely the values' order matches the order rows are stored in.

From those, the planner computes **selectivity**: the share of rows each condition keeps. Its weak spot is the assumption that conditions are **independent**: for `WHERE city = 'London' AND country = 'UK'` it multiplies the two selectivities and underestimates badly. **Extended statistics**, which describe how columns relate, fix that: `CREATE STATISTICS ... (dependencies, ndistinct, mcv) ON city, country FROM addresses`. For skewed columns, raise the per-column target: `ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET STATISTICS 1000`.

There are three ways to carry out a join:

- **Nested loop join**: for each row on the outer side, look up its matches, ideally through an index. Best when the outer side is small.
- **Hash join**: load the smaller input into a quick lookup structure (a **hash table**) kept in the server's memory, then check each row of the other against it. Good for large joins on equal values; needs memory (`work_mem`).
- **Merge join**: walk through two inputs sorted on the join column, side by side. Good when both are already sorted or very large.

The planner searches join orders exhaustively up to `join_collapse_limit` (8) tables; beyond `geqo_threshold` (12) a genetic search takes over.

A prepared statement (a query sent once and then run many times with different values) may switch after five runs to a reusable **generic plan** that ignores the actual values. That can hurt when some values are far more common than others; `plan_cache_mode` controls it.
takeaways: Plans are chosen by estimated cost; estimates come from pg_stats via ANALYZE
The planner assumes columns are unrelated, so conditions on related columns are misestimated; use CREATE STATISTICS
Nested loop for small outer sides, hash join for large equality joins, merge join for sorted inputs
Run ANALYZE after bulk loads
pitfalls: Bulk-loading a table and querying it immediately, before autovacuum has analysed it, with plans based on an empty table.

quiz.q: WHERE city = 'Paris' AND country = 'France' is estimated at 50 rows but returns 20,000. Best fix?
options: Create extended statistics (dependencies/mcv) on (city, country) and ANALYZE
quiz.explain: The planner multiplied two selectivities as if independent; extended statistics capture the dependency.

quiz.q: Which join method suits a small outer input with an index on the inner join column?
quiz.explain: Nested loop with an index lookup per outer row is cheapest when there are few outer rows.

concepts.name: Table partitioning
concepts.summary: Split very large tables into partitions by range, by list of values or evenly by a computed number, and drop old data instantly.
concepts.why: Partitioning keeps billion-row tables manageable and makes deleting old data instant instead of a day-long DELETE.
concepts.body:
**Declarative partitioning** splits one table into smaller child tables, called **partitions**, each holding part of the rows. Queries and writes go to the parent; PostgreSQL routes rows to the right partition.

```sql
CREATE TABLE events (...) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);
CREATE TABLE events_2026_03 PARTITION OF events
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-03-01') TO ('2026-04-01');
```

Range bounds include the lower and exclude the upper value. Other strategies: `PARTITION BY LIST (region)` for a fixed set of values, and `PARTITION BY HASH (customer_id)`, which spreads rows evenly by a number computed from the value. A `DEFAULT` partition catches rows that fit nowhere else (but it rules out `DETACH ... CONCURRENTLY`).

What you gain:

- **Partition pruning**: a query with `WHERE created_at >= '2026-03-10'` skips partitions that can't match, either while planning or, when the value is only known later, while running.
- **Cheap removal of old data**: removing a month is `DETACH PARTITION` plus `DROP TABLE`, which just deletes that partition's files, instead of deleting millions of rows one by one and cleaning up the leftovers afterwards. `DETACH ... CONCURRENTLY` (PostgreSQL 14+) does it without making queries wait.
- Smaller indexes, and cleanup that works on one partition at a time.

What it costs:

- Queries that do not filter on the partition key touch every partition.
- A primary key or `UNIQUE` rule must include the partition key columns, so an `id` that is unique across the whole table can't be enforced on its own.
- Each partition adds planning work; thousands of partitions slow down every query. Aim for partitions of a size that matches your retention or access unit, not as many as possible.
- New partitions must exist before data arrives; schedule their creation (the `pg_partman` extension automates it).

Partitioning is not a substitute for indexes. Below roughly hundreds of millions of rows, or without a clear key that queries filter on and data ages by, a well-indexed single table is usually simpler and as fast.
takeaways: RANGE, LIST and HASH partitioning; range upper bounds are excluded
Pruning skips partitions only when queries filter on the partition key
Detach and drop partitions for instant data retention
Unique keys must include the partition key; too many partitions slow planning
pitfalls: Partitioning on a column queries rarely filter by, so every query scans all partitions.

quiz.q: Why must the primary key of a range-partitioned events table include created_at?
options: Primary keys must contain a timestamp
PostgreSQL enforces uniqueness per partition, so the key must include the partitioning columns
quiz.explain: There are no global indexes; uniqueness is only guaranteed across partitions when the key determines the partition.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of DETACH + DROP over DELETE for removing a month of data?
options: It is a quick metadata operation that leaves no dead tuples to vacuum
quiz.explain: Dropping a partition removes its files at once; DELETE rewrites millions of tuples as dead versions.

concepts.name: Write-ahead log, backups and replication
concepts.summary: How the write-ahead log makes commits survive crashes, and how it powers backups that restore to any moment, and copies of the database.
concepts.why: Durability settings, backups, switching to a standby server and copies falling behind all follow from how the WAL works.
concepts.body:
PostgreSQL never writes a changed data page to disk before the change is noted in the **write-ahead log** (WAL): a file of change notes that only ever grows at the end. On `COMMIT`, only the WAL has to be forced onto disk (`fsync`); the changed data pages stay in the server's memory and are written later, in the background and at **checkpoints**, moments when everything changed so far is written out. Sequential WAL writes are much cheaper than scattered page writes, and that design gives you:

- **Crash recovery**: after a crash, PostgreSQL replays WAL from the last checkpoint. Committed transactions reappear; uncommitted ones never become visible.
- **Tunable durability**: `synchronous_commit = off` returns from `COMMIT` before the WAL flush. A crash can lose the last fraction of a second of commits, but never corrupts data. Useful for low-value, high-volume writes.
- **Checkpoint tuning**: `max_wal_size` and `checkpoint_timeout` trade write bursts against recovery time.

Because WAL describes every change, it can be shipped elsewhere.

- **Point-in-time recovery**: a **base backup** (a full copy of the data files, made with `pg_basebackup`) plus saved WAL files can be restored to any moment, such as one second before someone ran a bad `DELETE`. A `pg_dump` export is a copy as of one moment only: useful, but it can't go to any other point in time.
- **Streaming replication**: a **standby** server receives the WAL continuously and replays it, staying an exact copy. It can answer read-only queries (a hot standby) and take over if the main server fails.
- By default this is **asynchronous**: the main server doesn't wait for the standby, so replicas **lag** slightly behind, and taking over can lose the latest commits. `synchronous_standby_names` makes each commit wait for a standby, trading **latency** (each commit takes longer) for zero loss.
- **Logical replication**: sends the row changes of chosen tables to another server (it publishes; the other subscribes), even one running another major version. Useful for upgrades and feeding other systems.

**Replication slots** make the main server keep any WAL that a replica or other consumer hasn't received yet. An abandoned slot keeps WAL forever and will fill the disk; monitor it.
takeaways: Changes reach the WAL before data pages; COMMIT waits only for the WAL flush
Crash recovery replays WAL from the last checkpoint
Base backup + saved WAL = restore to any moment
Replicas lag behind by default; abandoned replication slots fill the disk
pitfalls: Treating a replica as a backup: a bad DELETE is copied to it within milliseconds.

quiz.q: What does synchronous_commit = off risk after a server crash?
options: Losing the most recent commits, without corruption
Losing all data since the last checkpoint, including committed rows
quiz.explain: COMMIT returns before the WAL flush, so the latest commits may be missing, but the database stays consistent.

quiz.q: Which setup can restore a database to the state just before an accidental DELETE at 14:03?
options: A base backup plus continuous WAL archiving
quiz.explain: Point-in-time recovery replays archived WAL on top of a base backup up to the chosen moment.

concepts.name: Performance tuning in practice
concepts.summary: A step-by-step way to find and fix a slow database: measure, read plans, fix queries, then tune the server.
concepts.why: Most slow live databases suffer from a few bad queries, missing indexes or badly set up connections, and measuring finds them.
takeaways: Measure with pg_stat_statements; optimise by total time, not just slowest single run
Most wins come from indexes, removing N+1 queries and better paging
work_mem applies per sort or hash step of each query; raise it for one connection, not for all
Pool connections and keep autovacuum ahead of bloat
pitfalls: Raising work_mem globally to fix one report and running the server out of memory under load.

quiz.q: Which query should you usually optimise first?
options: The one with the highest single execution time
The one with the highest total execution time across all calls
quiz.explain: Total time reflects real load: frequent cheap queries often dominate.

quiz.q: work_mem is 64MB and max_connections is 500. Why can this be dangerous?
options: work_mem is reserved at startup for each connection
work_mem limits the size of shared_buffers
Each sort or hash operation in each query may use up to work_mem, so peak usage can far exceed RAM
quiz.explain: The limit applies per operation, and many concurrent operations can each claim it.
